Course Description: Theory seminar taught alternate years. Study of analytical modeling techniques in accounting research that covers topics such as performance measurement for incentives, the consequences of asymmetric information in economic relationships and the role of accounting therein, and information sharing within and across firms.
faculty_bio: Jacob “Jake” Thomas is the Williams Brothers Professor of Accounting and Finance at Yale School of Management. His research and teaching focus on the relationship between accounting information, stock prices, equity valuation, financial management, and trading strategies. He helped develop Yale SOM’s core curriculum and has written cases and teaching materials for his courses. Before joining Yale, he was the Ernst & Young Professor of Accounting and Finance at Columbia Business School; he holds a PhD from the University of Michigan. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/jacob-thomas))

Course Description:
This course presents an introduction to asset pricing at the PhD level. The first half of the
course covers the theory of choice under uncertainty, then develops classical asset pricing
theory in discrete time, including the principle of no arbitrage, mean-variance analysis,
the CAPM, and factor models. The second half of the course will focus on the connection
between asset prices and macroeconomic quantities. After covering the main models
based on consumption data, we will move to production-based asset pricing and pricing
in the presence of various frictions. We will also cover optimal (short-run and especially
long-run) portfolio choice.
The course assumes knowledge of microeconomics and statistics at an advanced
undergraduate level, but does not require any prior knowledge of finance. It is aimed at
first-year PhD students in Financial Economics.
faculty_bio: Stefano Giglio is the Frederic D. Wolfe Professor of Finance, Management, and Entrepreneurship at Yale School of Management. His research focuses on asset pricing, macroeconomics, and climate finance, particularly ways to hedge crash, uncertainty, and climate risks. He teaches finance, including courses related to asset management and climate finance. Before joining Yale, he was an associate professor at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business and earned his PhD in economics from Harvard University. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/stefano-giglio))

Course Title: Financial Econometrics and Machine Learning Part 1
Course Description:
Empirical work is the foundation of great economics. Theory is also the foundation of great
economics. Theorists work on closing the gap between theory and reality. Empiricists are
explorers that map the unchartered territory between theory and reality. This is a division
of labor view of Popper’s philosophy of science. This course is designed to help build a skill
set for pushing the empirical side of this proposition, particularly tailored to asset pricing
research. This is in large part a course in advanced statistical methods for finance. It is not a facts
course. I will bring in many empirical facts as we go. But the more important take-away for
you is a set of methods you can you to discover your own new facts.
faculty_bio: Bryan T. Kelly is the Frederick Frank ’54 and Mary C. Tanner Professor of Finance at Yale School of Management, Associate Director of its International Center for Finance, a Research Fellow at the National Bureau of Economic Research, and head of machine learning at AQR Capital Management. His research focuses on asset pricing and financial econometrics, including financial machine learning, volatility and tail risk, systemic banking risk, financial intermediation, and financial networks. He previously taught as a tenured professor at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business and has published in leading economics and finance journals. Kelly earned degrees from the University of Chicago, UC San Diego, and NYU Stern, and worked in investment banking at Morgan Stanley before pursuing his PhD. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/bryan-t-kelly))

Course Description:
This course surveys corporate finance research at the PhD level, including classic
topics/papers and more recent developments. A typical class session will provide background and
context for a given topic and will talk about several papers in detail. Major topics covered will
include corporate capital structure, banking, corporate governance, executive compensation,
merger acquisitions, entrepreneurial finance, private equity, corporate innovation, and behavioral
corporate finance. Emphasis will be placed on recent empirical research, although we will also
cover fundamental theoretical insights.
faculty_bio: Song Ma is a Professor of Finance and Entrepreneurship at Yale School of Management, a Faculty Research Fellow at the National Bureau of Economic Research, and an affiliated faculty member at Yale Law School’s Center for the Study of Corporate Law and Yale SOM’s Program on Entrepreneurship. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/song-ma)) His research focuses on innovation economics, entrepreneurship, financial economics, artificial intelligence, and big data, with additional work in corporate strategy, antitrust, labor, and business law. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/song-ma)) He teaches courses including Entrepreneurial Finance, Venture Capital and Private Equity, and Finance and Society, and joined Yale SOM’s faculty in 2016. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/song-ma)) Ma earned a PhD in Finance from Duke University in 2016 and a BA in Economics from Zhejiang University in 2010. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/song-ma))

Alp Simsek is a Professor of Finance at Yale School of Management, where he has served since 2022. His research focuses on the connections between financial markets and the macroeconomy, including international finance, behavioral finance, beliefs, speculation, asset prices, monetary policy, and business cycles. Before Yale, he taught economics at MIT and Harvard, and he is a research associate at the National Bureau of Economic Research and a research affiliate at the Centre for Economic Policy Research. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/alp-simsek))

Course Description: The purpose of this seminar is to provide Ph.D.-level coverage of the psychology of decision making, focusing on choice. Although the normative issue of how choices should be made is relevant, the descriptive issue of how choices are made is the main focus of the course. In addition to examining prior choice research, the goal of this seminar is to improve your ability to identify interesting research questions and develop effective experiments for testing them. Students generally enroll from a variety of disciplines, including cognitive and social psychology, behavioral economics, finance, marketing, political science, medicine, and public health.
faculty_bio: Ravi Dhar is the George Rogers Clark Professor of Management and Marketing at Yale School of Management, director of the Yale Center for Customer Insights, and co-faculty leader of the Yale Program on Stakeholder Innovation and Management. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/ravi-dhar)) He also holds an affiliated professorship in psychology at Yale and focuses on consumer behavior, branding, marketing strategy, and the psychological factors shaping consumer decision-making. ([faculty.som.yale.edu](https://faculty.som.yale.edu/ravidhar/)) Dhar has published more than 70 articles, consulted for numerous Fortune 100 companies, and received honors including the Society for Consumer Psychology’s Distinguished Scientific Contribution Award. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/ravi-dhar)) His academic background includes a PhD and MS from the University of California, Berkeley, an MBA from the Indian Institute of Management, and a BTech from the Indian Institute of Technology. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/ravi-dhar))

Course Title: Current Topics in Judgement and Decision-Making
faculty_bio: Gal Zauberman is the Joseph F. Cullman 3rd Professor of Marketing at Yale School of Management. His research examines consumer judgment and decision-making, time perception, financial decision-making, the nature of experiences, and memory for emotions and choice. He earned a PhD from Duke University’s Fuqua School of Business in 2000 and a BA from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill in 1994, and has received several research awards, including the Early Career Award for Distinguished Contributions to Consumer Psychology. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/gal-zauberman))

Course Description:
This course covers analytical tools and topics that have not been discussed in previous
operations doctoral courses at Yale SOM. The emphasis is on approaches to modeling
and analyzing operational processes across various application areas, including supply
chains, service operations, retail operations, platform operations, and sustainable
operations. Students will explore key ideas and methodologies established in the
literature of Operations Research and Operations Management, understand the contexts
in which certain conventions have been developed, and learn how to build effective
mathematical models.  Part-1 and Part-2 can be taken independently. Students can enroll in both or only one.
faculty_bio: Uri Simonsohn is a Visiting Professor of Behavioral Science at Yale School of Management for the 2026–27 academic year and a Professor of Behavioral Science at ESADE Business School in Barcelona. His research focuses on judgment and decision-making, research methods, and the credibility and reproducibility of empirical findings. He teaches topics related to motivating behavioral change and improving people’s understanding of data through psychological research. Before joining ESADE, he was a professor at the Wharton School, where he served from 2003 to 2017. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/uri-simonsohn))

Course Description:
This course covers a wide range of models of operational processes with focus on physical
goods, which means that the course will not have much coverage of service processes.
Example of types of issues covered are key assumptions and setups, deterministic vs
uncertain demand, trade-off between too much and two little, short life-cycle products
vs long-term products with replenishment, multi-locations, vertical vs horizontal pricing,
delayed differentiation and modular product architecture, centralized and decentralized
decision making, bayesian updating of information and its influence on decisions.
faculty_bio: Nils Rudi is a Professor of Operations Management and Professor of Statistics and Data Science at Yale School of Management, where he earned his PhD from The Wharton School in 2000. His research focuses on managing uncertainty in supply chains and applying data-driven methods across areas including sports analytics, cognitive psychology, education, health care, and law. He teaches probability modeling, operational-process modeling, sports analytics, and a Yale Law School course on uncertainty, data, and judgment. Before academia, Rudi worked as a computer programmer and founded Minard, a decision-support company for forecasting and inventory management; he previously taught at the University of Rochester and INSEAD. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/nils-rudi))

faculty_bio: Zhen Lian is an Assistant Professor of Operations Management at Yale School of Management and a faculty fellow at Yale’s Center for Algorithms, Data, and Market Design. Her research focuses on optimization, transportation, public policy, and online marketplaces, particularly ridesharing and the gig economy. She teaches Operations Engine and Advanced Business Analytics, and previously worked as a postdoctoral fellow at Lyft on driver pay and incentive design. Lian holds a PhD from Cornell University and bachelor’s degrees from Peking University; she also helped redesign San Francisco school schedules, generating substantial transportation-cost savings. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/zhen-lian))

Course Title: Organizations and Management I: Inside Organizations
faculty_bio: Adriana L. Germano is an Assistant Professor of Organizational Behavior at Yale School of Management. Her research examines intergroup relations within organizations and society, focusing on how cultural norms shape group dynamics, gender and racial inequity, and workplace outcomes through experimental and observational methods. Before joining Yale, she was a postdoctoral research scholar at Columbia Business School and earned her Ph.D. in social psychology from the University of Washington. Her work has appeared in leading psychology journals, and she has received the SAGE Emerging Scholar Award and the Heritage Dissertation Award. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/adriana-l-germano))

Edward M. Watts is an Associate Professor of Accounting at the Yale School of Management. His research examines environmental, social, and governance (ESG) disclosures, investor behavior, market microstructure, and how information affects trading and market prices. He teaches Sustainable Investing and related courses on sustainable finance, stakeholder capitalism, and sustainability reporting. He earned a PhD from Stanford Graduate School of Business, an MA in Economics from Duke University, and a BA in Mathematics and Economics from SUNY Geneseo, and previously worked in fixed-income trading and investment banking at Morgan Stanley. Course Description: This is a short course on the theory and practice of leading, managing, and functioning in task-performing groups and teams. It has two primary goals: first, to provide students with a conceptual framework for analyzing group dynamics, diagnosing performance problems, and designing appropriate interventions, and second, to help students develop practical skills for building effective groups and teams. Both of these objectives are important to students’ effectiveness in study groups at SOM and in organizational teams they will join or lead after graduation. The design of the course is based on the belief that conceptual understanding of the principles of team effectiveness is of little use without a more direct experiential understanding of group dynamics (or process) and the behavioral skills required to implement this knowledge. This one-week course takes place the week following orientation. Course session times will be announced in Canvas.
Daytimes: M T W Th F 8:30 AM-4:30 PM
faculty_bio: Julia DiBenigno is a Professor of Organizational Behavior at Yale School of Management, with a courtesy appointment in Sociology. An organizational ethnographer and field researcher, she studies the sociology of work and occupations, collaboration across professional groups, upward influence and voice, and organizational change; she also teaches Managing Groups and Teams. Her background includes a PhD and MS from MIT Sloan, a summa cum laude psychology degree from Columbia, and prior consulting work in Deloitte’s Organization and Change practice. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/julia-dibenigno))

Course Description: The course helps students acquire basic accounting knowledge that is extremely useful in the day-to-day practice of general management. This basic accounting knowledge is indispensable background for the work to follow in the Organizational Perspectives courses as well as for elective courses in accounting, finance, marketing, and strategy. Accounting systems provide important financial information for all types of organizations across the globe. Despite their many differences, all accounting systems are built on a common foundation. Economic concepts, such as assets, liabilities, and income, are used to organize information into a fairly standard set of financial statements. Bookkeeping mechanics compile financial information with the double entry system of debits and credits. Accounting conventions help guide the application of the concepts through the mechanics. This course provides these fundamentals of accounting.
faculty_bio: Anya Nakhmurina is an Associate Professor of Accounting at the Yale School of Management. Her research examines the information environment of U.S. municipalities, especially financial-reporting transparency, municipal disclosures, governance, public finance, and cities’ climate-change adaptation and mitigation decisions. She earned a PhD in Accounting from the University of Chicago Booth School of Business and is an Affiliate Fellow of Booth’s Stigler Center for the Study of the Economy and the State. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/anya-nakhmurina))

Course Description: The ability to understand and apply probability concepts and statistical methods is fundamental to management education. The concepts covered in this course include probability, simulation, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, and applied regression modeling. Course Description: This course concentrates on the role of market processes in determining the opportunities facing individuals and business firms, the policy issues facing public officials, and the patterns of resource allocation in the economic system. It is intended to be accessible to students with little or no prior exposure to economics. The mathematical prerequisite is competence with basic algebra and calculus. The aim is to provide students with analytical tools to help them tackle economic problems, which arise whenever agents must make economic trade-offs or engage in trade. While we cover a range of topics in microeconomics, the emphasis throughout the course is on learning how to approach and tackle economic problems—a skill that will be useful in making managerial decisions. Topics include supply and demand, consumers, production, equilibrium, imperfect competition, competitive strategy.
faculty_bio: Kai Hao Yang is an Associate Professor of Economics at Yale School of Management. His research uses mechanism design and information design to study privacy, algorithmic fairness, price discrimination, consumer data, online platforms, political economy, and finance; he also teaches economics courses at Yale SOM. He earned a B.A. in Political Science from National Taiwan University and an M.A. and Ph.D. in Economics from the University of Chicago, and was previously a postdoctoral associate at Yale’s Cowles Foundation. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/kai-hao-yang))

Course Description:
This course is designed for students seeking a decisive competitive advantage by mastering the ability to both deploy and build custom AI agents for the modern enterprise. While the AI landscape is fast-evolving, the primary differentiator for future leaders is the transition from being a passive consumer of AI to an architect of AI-driven solutions.

The curriculum provides a rigorous, hands-on environment focused on fundamental, general-purpose AI building skills. Students move from theoretical understanding to the practical construction of tools using vibe coding and agentic frameworks. By the end of the thirteen sessions, students will have developed the technical intuition and engineering skills to build AI agents that integrate APIs, RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation), tool use, and autonomous workflows—skills that transfer across business functions and domains.
faculty_bio: Tauhid Zaman is an Associate Professor of Operations Management at Yale School of Management, where he also serves as Lecturer in Management and Special Advisor for AI Initiatives. His research uses probabilistic models, network algorithms, and modern statistical methods to address operational problems involving social-network data, including content popularity, online extremism, and user geolocation. He also studies data-driven startup investing, choice modeling, algorithmic sports betting, and biometric data. Zaman earned his BS, MEng, and PhD in electrical engineering and computer science from MIT, completing his doctorate in 2011. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/tauhid-zaman))

Course Description: This course equips students to use durable principles from economics, marketing, organizational behavior, accounting, and politics to achieve success in competitive environments.  Students will use course tools to understand a manager’s role in a company’s value creation and value capture activities.  Using this perspective, we will examine the potential for suppliers, buyers, complementors and traditional rivals to function as both competitors and cooperators to a company in the marketplace.    Emphasis will be placed on anticipating the actions of other marketplace participants by understanding those participants’ objectives and constraints.  The course explicitly recognizes that relevant players in the environment include governments, nonprofit organizations, and corporations and that all of these agents can behave both cooperatively and competitively.   Textbooks required for this course:  Microeconomics (Pindyck and Rubinfeld -whatever edition obtained for Economics is fine) and Coopetition (Brandenberger and Nalebuff).

Course Description: The course takes the viewpoint that the best way to create and keep a customer is to develop a deep understanding of customer behavior, integrate that understanding across the organization, and align the organizational structure to both satisfy current customer needs and adapt to changes in customer needs better than competitors. To be truly customer-focused and market-driven, a company (profit or nonprofit) should develop the capability to sense and respond to the changing needs of customers in the market. An important element of the course is the idea that customer focus must extend to the entire organization across all its major functions for it to be successful. The course consists of two main modules: (1) Understanding Customers and Creating a Superior Value Proposition and (2) Creating and Maintaining a Customer-Aligned Organization. The first module focuses on understanding customer needs in consumer and industrial markets from a multidisciplinary perspective (economics, psychology, and sociology) to create a superior value proposition; the second highlights how creating a customer-aligned organization requires functional perspectives that span marketing, operations, accounting, finance, and human resource management. Recommended Reading:  Marketing Management, 4/E, Russ Winer, New York University, Ravi Dhar, Yale University, ISBN-10: 0136074898, ISBN-13:  9780136074892
faculty_bio: Jiwoong Shin is a Professor of Marketing at Yale School of Management and Senior Editor at *Marketing Science*. His research focuses on marketing strategy, applied economic theory, and digital markets, including advertising, pricing, targeting, customer relationship management, and AI-mediated competition. He holds a Ph.D. in Management Science from MIT and MS and BS degrees from Seoul National University, and his teaching has earned Yale’s Inspiring Yale Award. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/jiwoong-shin))

The course consists of two main modules: (1) Understanding Customers and Creating a Superior Value Proposition and (2) Creating and Maintaining a Customer-Aligned Organization. The first module focuses on understanding customer needs in consumer and industrial markets from a multidisciplinary perspective (economics, psychology, and sociology) to create a superior value proposition; the second highlights how creating a customer-aligned organization requires functional perspectives that span marketing, operations, accounting, finance, and human resource management. Recommended Reading:  Marketing Management, 4/E, Russ Winer, New York University, Ravi Dhar, Yale University, ISBN-10: 0136074898, ISBN-13:  9780136074892

Course Description: This course is about investors: what they do, how they think, and what they care about. The course is, in places, quantitative. Course topics include returns, risk, and prices; asset allocation; efficient markets; valuation and fundamentals-based investing; the capital asset pricing model (CAPM); quantitative equity investing; bond markets; evaluating money manager performance; futures and options; and investment errors and human psychology.

Beinecke Professor of Finance and Management Studies at Yale School of Management, where he also serves as Faculty Director of the International Center for Finance and the Asset Management Curriculum. Course Description: Firms need governments to protect property rights, enforce contracts, mitigate market failures, and maintain an environment that is conducive to doing business. Governments depend on the private sector for investment, employment, and revenue, and sometimes to mitigate political failures. Future managers and leaders of both for-profit and non-profit private sector entities must understand the ways in which their organization’s mission is dependent on government and devise appropriate strategies vis-à-vis the public sector. Conversely, future public sector leaders must be cognizant of the effects of government action on business. This course is designed to expose students to frameworks derived primarily from the fields of economics and political science that help us analyze the social and political environments within which business operates. The first half of the course focuses on analyzing how government institutions affect the conduct of business and how business can shape government and policy. The second half does deeper dives into a number of pressing policy issues (such as gender and racial discrimination, immigration policy, education policy, public health in light of the COVID-19 epidemic, and the role of evidence in policymaking) that have large effects on employees, managers, shareholders, and other stakeholders. Beyond political science and economics, a rigorous analysis of these topics will require us to also draw on scholarship from the fields of law, history and sociology.
faculty_bio: Mushfiq Mobarak is the Jerome Kasoff ’54 Professor of Management and Economics at Yale School of Management, with a joint appointment in Yale’s Department of Economics. He is a development economist whose research uses field experiments to study how people in developing countries adopt welfare-improving technologies and behaviors, as well as how effective interventions can be scaled. He founded and directs the Yale Research Initiative on Innovation and Scale (Y-RISE), and teaches State & Society and Development Economics. His previous affiliations include the World Bank, IMF, Innovations for Poverty Action, J-PAL at MIT, and the International Growth Centre at LSE. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/ahmed-mushfiq-mobarak))

Course Description: This course is designed to provide students with a set of practical but powerful statistical methods valuable across a range of professional and personal settings. We being with data structure, sampling methodologies and data quality, then introduce advanced tools such as nonparametric regression and density estimation, quantile regression, maximum likelihood estimation and limited dependent variable models. Finally, we turn to causal inference: many of the most important questions in business, public policy and beyond often revolve around understanding how some variable X affects some other variable Y (e.g., how does demand for my product respond to a change in price; does microfinance reduce poverty; will drinking a glass of wine a day affect my life expectancy). We examine when and how data can be used to infer causality, using techniques such as regression discontinuity designs, matching estimators, instrumental variables, synthetic controls, differences-in-differences (...-in differences), event studies, randomized controlled trials and A/B testing. The emphasis will be on understanding the underlying concepts, and the practical use, implications and limitations of these techniques.

He has conducted research in China, the Dominican Republic, Mexico, Nepal, and India, and holds a PhD from Princeton University. Course Description:
Application Deadline 11:59 pm on Monday, June 30, 2026. The Impact Practicum is an elective course at the School of Management that offers an opportunity for students to receive course credit and faculty oversight for a professional consulting project that they want to pursue during the fall semester. Applications will be considered from students from all Yale graduate schools.

Projects could arise from a number of sources, including: serving on the board of a local nonprofit through the Nonprofit Board Fellows club; ongoing work with a local organization through the Social Impact Consulting club or Inclusive Growth Fellowship; a summer internship; opportunities that surface through other courses or professional affiliations. (Note: If you are being paid for your work, you would not be eligible for the course.)

The goal of the course is to provide a structure, process, and frameworks for students’ consulting projects to ensure that they are carried out in a rigorous manner with clear milestones and deliverables. The course will have one weekly class session and one weekly meeting with a faculty mentor.
faculty_bio: Tony Sheldon is a Senior Lecturer in the Practice of Management and Senior Advisor to Yale SOM’s Program on Social Enterprise, Innovation, and Impact, having served as the program’s executive director from 2008 to 2025. He teaches practicum courses on social entrepreneurship, with student teams supporting organizations in countries including Brazil, Kenya, and the United States. His professional and research interests center on international development, microfinance, social performance management, and collaboration to address complex social problems. Sheldon holds an M.P.P.M. from Yale SOM and an A.B. from Princeton University. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/tony-sheldon))

Course Description: The purpose of this course is to study, discuss, and debate many issues of concern to managers of nonprofit organizations. Broadly speaking, these issues involve mission definition, competing internal and external demands, resource scarcity and uncertainty, governance systems, and managing strategic change. While the principal thrust of the course is on nonprofit organizations, there will be opportunities to examine areas where public, for-profit, and nonprofit organizations interact. The course is primarily, although not exclusively, a case-based course.
faculty_bio: Judith Chevalier is the William S. Beinecke Professor of Finance and a Professor of Economics at Yale University, with an appointment at Yale School of Management. Her research focuses on industrial organization, retail and online markets, consumer behavior, and pricing, and she teaches economics and finance-related courses. She earned her Ph.D. from MIT and is recognized for scholarship on competition and firm strategy in evolving markets. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty/judith-chevalier))

Course Description:
Applications for GSE India are open from Monday, June 1, 2026 until Friday, June 12, 2026. The link to the application is here.
Launched in 2008 at the Yale School of Management, the Global Social Entrepreneurship (GSE) India course links teams of Yale students with social enterprises based in India. GSE is committed to channeling the skills of Yale students to assist Indian organizations to expand their reach and impact on “base of the pyramid” communities. Yale students partner with mission-driven social entrepreneurs (SEs) to focus on a specific management challenge that the student/SE teams work together to address during the semester.  GSE has worked with more than 50 leading and emerging Indian social enterprises engaged in economic development, sustainable energy, women’s empowerment, education, environmental conservation, and affordable housing. The course covers both theoretical and practical issues, including case studies and discussions on social enterprise, developing a theory of change and related social metrics, financing social businesses, the role of civil society in India, framing a consulting engagement, managing team dynamics, etc. The course will be taught by Asha Ghosh, Lecturer at SOM. The course meets on Wednesday afternoons 2:40 – 5:40 during Fall-2 and Spring-1. Students will travel to India to work on-site with their partner SEs, and for a convening of all the student/SE project teams, in mid- to late January 2026 for 10 days. As with the International Experience and the Global Network Immersion Week, students will be responsible for covering the costs of their round-trip airfare to India and related expenses (such as visa and immunizations). SOM students can draw on their available GSA days to offset in-country travel, hotel, and related costs. GSE has arrangements with Jackson and YSE to cover in-country costs for their students. Enrollment is by application only. Students accepted and enrolled in GSE will allocate 150 of their fall course bidding points towards the course. This is considered a 6 unit course that spans fall-2 and spring-1. It may not be taken as a half semester course. 2 units are applied in fall-2 and 4 units applied in spring-1.  If travel to India is cancelled the units will change from 4 to 2 in spring 2026.
faculty_bio: Asha Ghosh is a Lecturer in the Practice of Management at Yale School of Management, where she teaches Global Social Entrepreneurship in India. Her research interests include poverty alleviation, urban politics and policy, and community engagement in Asia. Before joining Yale, she worked in international development focused on decentralization and local governance in Asia and served as YSE’s Urban Program Manager from 2019 to 2024; she holds degrees from MIT and Tufts University. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/asha-ghosh))

Course Description:
Attendance is required for the first two classes to retain a place in the course or on the waiting list. This course has a mandatory weekly lab meeting and a mandatory off-campus weekend retreat (see important dates for the 2025-2026 academic calendar at https://faculty.som.yale.edu/heidibrooks/interpersonal-and-group-dynamics/). 
Amidst an epidemic of loneliness and rising levels of burnout—often fueled by interpersonal stressors at work—our capacity to build meaningful connections is essential. Studies have shown that the average manager spends about two-thirds of their time interacting with others. It should be no surprise that skill in interpersonal relationships is one of the most frequent determinants of managerial success or failure. This course is designed to help students learn some of the skills necessary for successfully navigating and leading in the face of fast-paced, complex human interaction. The central focus is to increase students' ability to understand and diagnose interpersonal dynamics as well as to increase personal understanding of how they impact others.
This course is a memory-making, powerful and even transformational experience for many students. While readings and group exercises are used to begin discussion, the core learning material emerges in small group interaction. Students learn how they function in small groups and how they relate to others from feedback and reaction of other class members. As such, students planning to enroll should understand that the course methodologies are likely quite different than most courses you have taken to date. Much of the learning will emerge from a) personal reflection on interpersonal and group dynamics and b) the ability/willingness to learn interpersonally from experience, risk-taking, self-disclosure, and feedback.
Interested students are encouraged to attend the first session to better understand this unique course experience.  Attendance is required for the first two classes to retain a place in the course or on the waiting list. Note that the first assignment requires screening for this course. More information available at https://faculty.som.yale.edu/heidibrooks/
faculty_bio: Heidi Brooks is a Senior Lecturer in Organizational Behavior at Yale School of Management and directs Yale SOM’s Program for the Practice of Everyday Leadership. Her teaching and advising focus on everyday leadership, interpersonal and group dynamics, and the social interactions through which people shape meaning, influence one another, and work together. She holds a doctorate in psychology from the University of California, Berkeley, and a bachelor’s degree from Brown University. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/heidi-brooks))

Course Description: Business is an activity in which parties exchange goods or services for valuable consideration. The goal of this course is to examine the ethical dimensions of such activities and develop skills for identifying and weighting ethical considerations. The aims are twofold. One, we will discover the tools we use for reasoning about right and wrong at the individual, firm, and policy levels. Discussion and debate about the readings, including on Canvas forums, are a frequent part of the course. Two, we will explore “blind spots” – reasons why people fail to see the ethical dimension of decisions and thus, how they fail to live up to their own ethical standards.
faculty_bio: Corey Cusimano is an Assistant Professor of Marketing at Yale School of Management. His research examines everyday metacognition—how people understand and evaluate reasoning when forming judgments or making choices—as well as consumer values, morality, charitable behavior, and evaluations of corporate conduct. Before joining Yale SOM, he was a postdoctoral scholar at Princeton University’s University Center for Human Values. He holds a PhD in Experimental Psychology from the University of Pennsylvania and bachelor’s degrees in Philosophy and Psychology from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/corey-cusimano))

Jason Dana is an Associate Professor of Management at Yale School of Management and a member of its Behavioral Science faculty. His research examines judgment and decision-making in social and organizational contexts, including moral behavior, cooperation, and strategic interaction. He teaches behavioral science and holds a PhD in psychology from Harvard University. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/jason-dana))

Two, we will explore “blind spots” – reasons why people fail to see the ethical dimension of decisions and thus, how they fail to live up to their own ethical standards.

Course Description: This is a semester long course that provides an examination of current theory, research and policy on urban poverty and regional economic development in the U.S., as a background for economic development interventions in city and community settings. The course topics include: (1) measurements and theoretical explanations of poverty, incorporating both panel data and ethnography; (2) analytic tools for assessing community and regional economic flows; and (3) strategies for economic development and wealth building in urban populations and communities. We examine innovative approaches in the traditional areas of economic development practice including: strategies for revitalizing the regional economic base, business creation and development, workforce development and skills training, housing, education, and financial services. Strategies we explore include: cluster based economic development, place-based anchor strategies, sectoral workforce development training, affordable housing and community land trusts, neighborhood revitalization, and business development. By the end of the semester, students will: 1. Develop an understanding of the portfolio of theories, tools and strategies for regional economic development for urban regions in United States; 2. Build technical skills to analyze the economic base of a regional economy and apply these skills to a region of their choosing; 3. Build technical skills to analyze the demographic base of a regional economy and apply these skills to a region of their choosing; 4. Develop an understanding of the historic forces shaping the current material conditions of unequal economic development across regional geographies and demographic groups as it relates to particular regions of the U.S. metropole; 5. Critically evaluate a range of approaches to economic development (informed by learning goals 1-4) and analyze their utility for a specific region; 6. Design a communication tool using two formats (Ted talk, opED) to showcase an innovative approach to economic development exploring its potential for application in a specific US context.
faculty_bio: Kate Cooney is a Senior Lecturer in Social Enterprise and Management at Yale School of Management and the founding director of its Inclusive Economic Development Lab. Her research examines the intersection of business and social sectors, with current interests including social finance, inclusive economic development in American cities, and social-sector data visualization and storytelling. She teaches community economic development and urban poverty, previously served on the Boston University faculty, and holds a PhD and MSW from UCLA’s Luskin School of Public Affairs. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/kate-cooney))

Course Title: Inequality and Social Mobility: Understanding Opportunity in the Age of AI
Course Description:
Why do some people move up the economic ladder while others do not? How do education, family background, labor markets, public policy, and technology shape economic opportunity?
This course examines inequality and social mobility in the United States and around the world through a data-driven lens. We will study how income, wealth, race, gender, geography, education, labor-market institutions, and technological change influence economic opportunity and the distribution of resources across generations. Topics include intergenerational mobility, segregation, education, taxation and redistribution, globalization, the future of work, and the role of firms and public institutions in expanding opportunity.
Drawing on frontier economic research and empirical case studies, students will learn to evaluate evidence, assess competing explanations for economic disparities, and analyze policies designed to promote opportunity. AI will be integrated throughout the course as a tool for research, analysis, and communication, while also serving as a lens through which to examine the future of work and economic mobility.
faculty_bio: Barbara Biasi is an Associate Professor of Economics at Yale School of Management. Her research lies in labor and public economics, with a focus on education, including teacher compensation, school finance, educational inequality, and the allocation of resources across schools and students. She earned her PhD from Stanford University in 2017 and is also a Faculty Research Fellow at the National Bureau of Economic Research. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/barbara-biasi))

Course Description:
Interpersonal influence isn’t rocket science but it’s a science. It’s not magic but as you learn to apply the science it’ll sometimes feel like a superpower. In this course, you’ll study influence strategies that feel comfortable on both sides so that you can be persuasive without being manipulative. Drawing on research from social psychology, behavioral economics, and neuroscience, you’ll be deepening your knowledge through readings and class discussions, then conducting your own experiments in real-world challenges. Your synthesis of knowledge and practice will leave you better equipped to get job offers, fund startups, collaborate with teams, negotiate deals, influence policies, smooth disagreements, improve your relationships, amplify your activism, and connect with people.

We do a lot in 7 weeks! You’ll hit the ground running with deliverables due Mon/Wed/Fri, beginning immediately. Expect readings, challenges, and deliverables to take 5-10h/week. You’ll also participate in an evening challenge and publish an article. And if you put in the effort, you’ll have fun and make some friends :-)

Set the stage for achieving your goals through ongoing mastery of influence and persuasion in a boot camp-style intensive course. Help you become a person people increasingly want to say yes to.    Whether you have formal authority or not, your effectiveness as a leader and change agent depends on your ability to influence others to want to follow you. To want to say Yes. In this boot camp practicum, you'll study research findings and discuss tools like handling resistance and using other people's standards for themselves, but the real work and real benefit happens outside of class. You'll put influence into practice with weekly G-Force challenges to help you gain useful skills, shift your thinking, and build resilience. Although you'll learn some red flags to watch out for so you can protect yourself against would-be manipulators, and we'll discuss how to handle difficult people, we focus on making influence more comfortable and fun for all parties. Because then you'll be more likely to use it. Which means you'll be a stronger leader, better able to shape the world around you. Research shows nice people DO finish first—but ""nice"" might be different from what you thought. 

Find out for yourself.

Her research focuses on persuasion, decision-making, behavior change, and well-being. Before Yale, she managed a $200 million segment of Mattel’s Barbie brand, developed an executive education leadership program at Harvard, and worked as an actor and entrepreneur. She holds a doctorate from Harvard, an MBA from the University of Southern California, and a bachelor’s degree from Haverford College. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/zoe-chance))

Course Description: It is not always possible to make products better, but it is often possible to make them appear better so that consumers will choose them. Building on this idea, this course explores how to understand and influence consumer behavior. We will discuss how to capture consumers’ attention, shape their perceptions, and guide their decisions. Along the way, we will cover topics with important implications for both business (e.g., advertising, branding, pricing, and choice structuring) and society (e.g., saving, exercising, eating healthy, donating, and going green). Each class will combine theoretical foundations with practical applications.

Course Description: This course offers students the opportunity to develop skills and acquire experience in dealing with strategic marketing problems. The course aimes at helping students look at the entire marketing mix in light of the strategy of the firm. The course builds on the foundation developed in core courses, and the basic framework rests on the recent development in economics and strategy – resource based view (RBV) of strategy. You will have a chance to illustrate your ability to apply this framework in this course through case discussion and an in-class final exam. It will be most helpful to students pursuing careers in which they need to look at the firm as a whole. Examples include consultants, investment analysts, entrepreneurs, and product managers. Case studies will highlight marketing strategy exercise in consumer packaged goods, high tech, pharmaceuticals, and luxury goods.

Course Description: This lecture course offers an overview of all aspects of energy systems and their interaction with society and the environment. The course provides students with a comprehensive theoretical and empirical knowledge base about energy systems in the world. This course describes and explains the basics of energy and the laws that govern it, the different components of an energy system (supply technologies, delivery systems, and demand), the institutions that govern the energy sectors, the role of energy in development, its impact on climate change, and an understanding of the key challenges of an energy transition towards a sustainable future. The course has a specific emphasis on electricity systems, how they are operated and governed, and how they have to be transformed to tackle climate change. Students receive a unique exposure to energy issues in the Global South. This course provides students with basic analytical tools and knowledge to formulate and solve energy-related decisions at an individual, national, and global scale and to understand and critique ongoing policy dialogues on energy and climate. This course is cross-listed with the School of the Environment and follows the YSE academic calendar.

Course Description:
Please note that full attendance in the first and last classes are required to get credit for the course. Additionally, please note that there will be an assignment due prior to the first class. Auditing is not permitted.

Finance can be likened to the circulatory system of the global economy, and we will focus on the past, present and future of that system. The course is designed to deal with questions such as these: What is the global financial system and how does it work? What are the pressures on that system including market, regulatory, political and social dynamics? What are the key challenges to that system? How can the system be strengthened? In this course we are defining the global financial system (GFS) as encompassing central banks, commercial banks, and other financial institutions such as asset managers and private equity firms, financial regulators and international organizations. Thus, we will encompass subjects such as the U.S. Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, Goldman Sachs and the Hong Kong Shanghai Bank, the Carlyle Group and the BlackRock Investment Management Co., the Financial Stability Oversight Council and the Financial Stability Board, the Bank for International Settlements and the International Monetary Fund. We will take a broad view of the GFS including its history, its geopolitical framework, its economic foundations and its legal underpinnings. We will consider the GFS as a critical public good in the same way that clean air is a public good. We will look at a number of other key issues such as how the GFS deals with economic growth, economic and financial stability, distributional questions, employment issues, and long-term investments in infrastructure. We will discuss how new technologies are affecting several of the biggest issues in global finance. We will examine the GFS as a large-scale complex network, thereby compelling us to see it in an interconnected and multidisciplinary way. The emphasis will be on the practice of global finance more than the theory.
faculty_bio: Jeffrey E. Garten is Dean Emeritus and Juan Trippe Professor in the Practice Emeritus of International Trade, Finance, and Business at Yale School of Management, where he has taught since serving as dean from 1995 to 2005. His teaching focuses on global finance and global business, including financial centers, China’s role in the global economy, and leading multinational companies. Before joining Yale, Garten was U.S. Under Secretary of Commerce for International Trade and spent 13 years on Wall Street, including roles at Lehman Brothers and the Blackstone Group. He holds a PhD and MA from Johns Hopkins University and a BA from Dartmouth College. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/jeffrey-e-garten))

Course Description:
This course is open to all Yale graduate students as well as Yale College seniors. Full attendance in the first and last classes are required to get credit for the course. Also, please note that there is a homework assignment due before the first class. Auditing is not permitted.
Course description: This course will be co-taught by Jeffrey E. Garten and Robert D. Hormats, whose combined experience spans the Nixon, Ford, Carter, Reagan, Clinton, and Obama administrations, as well as decades on Wall Street. The course is based on the premise that America's role and policies in the global economy are undergoing a profound change that will outlast the current administration in Washington. It will examine the major forces in the U.S. and abroad that will be determining America's future in the global economy and the likely policies it will follow for the next decade. These will include changes in the country's industrial and financial structures, new social pressures, new demographic patterns, and evolving political alignments. Typical of the kinds of questions to be examined will be: How will the changing labor force affect America's interest in the global arena? How will changing technology affect these interests? What about changes in energy and the environment? What will trade policy, policy toward foreign investment and immigration policy look like? How should we think about the changing roles of Wall Street, Corporate America, and Silicon Valley? Regarding developments abroad, we will ask questions such as these: How will China's evolving interests, or new directions for the European Union, or the changing position of big emerging markets, or new pressures in global finance influence American policy, and with what effect? If the U.S. attempts to reduce its international involvement, who will write and try to enforce the "rules of the game?" Given the centrality of the United States to the global economy, the course will be important global background for future leaders in any profession. SEE SYLLABUS.

Course Description: This course is about the economics of competition law and policy. We will analyze and discuss how US antitrust laws, as applied and interpreted by agencies and courts, place limits on firm behavior.  We will study economic theories underlying antitrust enforcement and consider whether legal rules restricting competitive behavior make economic sense and how they affect managerial choices. We will discuss the evidence and reasoning advanced in key antitrust cases, and consider how case outcomes may affect social welfare and firm strategies. The course will also cover the procedures, standards, and recent outcomes in the EU’s Competition Authority.  Current enforcement cases will be integrated into the syllabus as they appear in the news.   The course is open to undergraduate students who have taken Intermediate Microeconomics and Law students with an economics background. The SOM calendar does not line up exactly with the College or Law School. If we find that these calendars create a conflict with our class, I will run a makeup session for the affected students.
faculty_bio: Fiona Scott Morton is the Theodore Nierenberg Professor of Economics at Yale School of Management. Her research and teaching focus on industrial organization, antitrust, competition policy, and strategy, particularly in technology markets. She previously served as Chief Economist of the U.S. Department of Justice’s Antitrust Division and earned her Ph.D. in economics from MIT. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/fiona-scott-morton))

Doug Kysar is the Joseph M. Field ’55 Professor of Law at Yale Law School. His research and teaching focus on torts, environmental law, climate change, and the regulation of risk. He holds degrees from Harvard University and Yale Law School and has served on the Yale faculty since 2000. ([law.yale.edu](https://law.yale.edu/doug-kysar))

Course Description:
AM required (AM student pre-registered). This course delves into quantitative factor investing, the basic building blocks of quantitative models of
investing. We will explore the scientific evidence and theory behind factor investing and examine its
applications, including index funds, smart beta, quantitative hedge fund models, and performance evaluation.
The course is primarily empirically focused with heavy data applications. Students will replicate studies and
design their own tests of theories and apply them to the data. Attention will also be paid to how these concepts
fit within the theoretical paradigms of risk-based and behavioral asset pricing theory.
faculty_bio: Tobias J. Moskowitz is the Theodore O. Yntema Professor of Finance at Yale School of Management and a research associate at the National Bureau of Economic Research. His research focuses on empirical asset pricing, behavioral finance, and the economics of sports, and he teaches finance and investment-related courses. Policy modeling refers to applications of operations research and allied quantitative methods to policy problems. Policy modeling is most useful when the amounts of data, money, time, and other resources one would like for purely scientific investigation are highly constrained by the decision-making environment. Recognizing that analyses of all sorts often exhibit diminishing returns in insight to effort, the idea is to capture key features of various policy issues with relatively simple "first-strike" models that provide support for decision making. Building on earlier coursework in probability modeling, this course introduces a toolkit of such models, including optimization, cost-benefit and cost-effectiveness analysis, Bernoulli processes, hazard and duration models, random incidence, Markov models, queueing and fluid models, and algorithms—and shows how to apply them to policy questions.
The course will feature applications to problems drawn from public health, criminal justice, public housing, education, and other areas of public policy. Students will be responsible for attending all classes and participating in class discussions. There will be problem sets, which must be submitted on time to receive credit, and a few short in-class quizzes (see the syllabus for details). There is NO final exam. 
Prerequisite: Students must have completed MGT 403 (Probability Modeling and Statistics) or equivalent to take this class. The probability modeling knowledge required is covered in any introductory probability course and includes: sample space, event probabilities including marginal, joint and conditional, Bayes' Rule, random variables, probability distributions, expected value, mean, variance, Bernoulli, binomial, uniform, and normal random variables, independence, covariance and correlation, and sums of random variables (both independent and dependent). Policy modeling is not a class in statistics or econometrics.
faculty_bio: Faidra Monachou is an Assistant Professor of Operations Management at Yale School of Management and a Faculty Fellow at Yale’s Center for Algorithms, Data, and Market Design. Her research examines market design, its theoretical foundations, and applications to public policy, with a particular focus on education operations; she also teaches operations management, policy modeling, and doctoral courses in operations. She earned a Ph.D. in Management Science and Engineering from Stanford University and was a postdoctoral fellow at Harvard University. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/faidra-monachou))

Course Description: All public leaders must make choices that challenge their code of ethics. Sometimes, a chance of life or death is literally at stake: how and when should a leader decide to let some people die, or explicitly ask people to die to give others a chance to live? At other times, while life or death may not be at stake, a leader must still decide difficult issues: when to partner with unsavory characters, when to admit failure, when to release information or make choices transparent. The pandemic, the war in Ukraine, and continued instability around the world all make clearer than ever the consequences of decisions in one community that can affect the entire world. This interdisciplinary seminar draws on perspectives from law, management, and public policy in exploring how leaders develop their principles, respond when their principles fail or conflict, and make real-world choices when, in fact, there are no good choices. This course is cross-listed with the Jackson School of Global Affairs and follows their academic calendar.

Course Description:
This is not your usual start-up course. This is a course about how to be entrepreneurial in reducing health disparities and achieving public health goals. This includes both non-profit and for-profit entrepreneurship; and intrapreneurship, which means innovating within existing institutions (government agencies, non-profits, for-profits). We also focus heavily on extrapreneurship, which is the idea of innovating across the boundaries of multiple institutions.

The course is centered on health equity, which means that everyone has a fair and just opportunity to be as healthy as possible. This requires addressing obstacles to health such as poverty, racism, gender and other biases and their consequences; including disparities in power, livelihood, education, housing, food, safety, and health care services. We refer to these as drivers of health. Across careers and professions, our work influences and is influenced by one or more drivers of health.

In this case-based course, we examine a wide spectrum of public health entrepreneurship and intrapreneurship (PHEI) cases ranging from collective action in a non-profit setting to digital start-ups in a venture-backed setting. This course brings together students from the Schools of Management, Public Health, Environment, Global Affairs, Divinity, Engineering, Arts and Sciences, and undergraduates. There are no prerequisites, all are welcome.
faculty_bio: Teresa Chahine is a Senior Lecturer in Social Entrepreneurship at Yale School of Management and Faculty Director of the Social Innovation Initiative at Yale Jackson School of Global Affairs. She teaches social entrepreneurship and researches tools for advancing social and environmental determinants of health, including how to finance, measure, and scale social impact. Chahine previously launched a public-health entrepreneurship program at Harvard and founded Lebanon’s first venture-philanthropy organization. She is also the author of *Social Entrepreneurship: Building Impact Step by Step*. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/teresa-chahine))

Course Title: Housing Connecticut: Developing Healthy and Sustainable Neighborhoods
Course Description: Enrollment in this course is by application. Please submit this application: https://yale.qualtrics.com/jfe/form/SV_4NqusdIQnvCtAHk. This application is for SOM students only. Deadline to apply: Round 1 opens July 13th, seats offered July 28th, deadline to accept 8/3, Round 2 if seats available Class space limited, projected Enrollment: 12 Architecture, 6 Law, 6 SOM, 6 YSE SOM prerequisites: Please indicate in your statement of interest how this course will build on previous course work or work experience. SOM Lead Professor: Kate Cooney For other professional schools, please contact the lead faculty and apply through those school processes: LAW: Anika Singh Lemar, anika.lemar@ylsclinics.org ARCH: Andrei Harwell, andrei.harwell@yale.edu YSE: Aicha Woods, aicha.woods@yale.edu In this interdisciplinary clinic taught between the School of Architecture, School of Law, School of Management, and School of Environment and organized by the Yale Urban Design Workshop, students will gain hands-on, practical experience in architectural and urban development and social entrepreneurship while contributing novel, concrete solutions to the housing affordability crisis in Connecticut. Working in teams directly with local community-based non-profits, students will co-create detailed development proposals and architectural designs anchored by affordable housing, but which will also engage with a range of community development issues including environmental justice, sustainability, resilience, social equity, identity, food scarcity, mobility, and health. Through seminars and workshops with Yale faculty and guest practitioners, students will be introduced to the history, theory, issues, and contemporary practices in the field, and will get direct feedback on their work. Offered in partnership with the Connecticut Department of Housing (DOH) as part of the Connecticut Plan for Healthy Cities, student projects will center on community wealth building and equitable economic recovery in some of Connecticut’s most economically distressed neighborhoods, by proposing multi-sector, place-based projects that focus on housing, health, and economic development. Proposals will have the opportunity to receive funding from the State both towards the implementation of rapidly deployed pilot projects during the course period, as well as towards predevelopment activities for larger projects, such as housing rehabilitation or new building construction. Students in the course will be organized into multi-disciplinary teams including law, management, environment, and architecture students, who will ideate together and take on specific team roles, modeling real-world project development teams. Teams will be assigned to work with non-profit developers tackling development or redevelopment projects that include affordable housing. Facilities of the Yale Urban Design Workshop will be available to students of the course. Students may have the opportunity to continue their leadership in these projects following the end of the course, in a professional capacity, as they move towards implementation. Students will interact with their nonprofit partners, the Connecticut Commissioner of Housing, Connecticut Housing Finance Authority, and the Connecticut Green Bank.
faculty_bio: Kate Cooney is a Senior Lecturer in Social Enterprise and Management at Yale School of Management and the founding director of its Inclusive Economic Development Lab. Her research examines the intersection of business and social sectors, with current interests including social finance, inclusive economic development in American cities, and social-sector data visualization and storytelling. She teaches community economic development and urban poverty, previously served on the Boston University faculty, and holds a PhD and MSW from UCLA’s Luskin School of Public Affairs. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/kate-cooney))

Course Title: Topics in Advanced Management for Business & Society
Course Description: This course explores how advanced managers navigate the most consequential forces shaping business and society today. Building on the foundations students bring from their prior MBA training, the course examines a rotating set of contemporary challenges—drawn from areas such as emerging technologies, sustainable development, global trade, public health, and the broader social responsibilities of enterprise. Topics vary from year to year to reflect the issues most relevant to current global conditions, and may be addressed through faculty lectures, guest experts from industry and policy, and applied team projects. Throughout, students are asked to think critically about how leaders create value while serving the wider interests of society. The aim is to equip emerging global leaders to engage thoughtfully and act effectively amid uncertainty and rapid change.
faculty_bio: Robert T. Jensen is a Professor of Economics at the Yale School of Management and previously served as a professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania. His research focuses on poverty and economic development, particularly gender, health, education, fertility, and the role of markets and private enterprise. He has conducted research in China, the Dominican Republic, Mexico, Nepal, and India, and holds a PhD from Princeton University. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/robert-t-jensen))

Course Description:
Empirical Strategy with AI is an interactive, project-based course designed to equip students with hands-on experience applying quantitative methods to real-world business problems. Students will extensively use AI tools and large-scale datasets that cannot be efficiently analyzed on personal machines, instead leveraging Yale SOM’s high-performance computing resources. Essentially, this course places topics covered in our core and elective strategy classes “on the computer.” We’ll use big data to answer questions that managers routinely face, such as: Where are there growth opportunities? How substitutable are different products? What prices should firms charge?

The curriculum emphasizes the practical use of AI to analyze real business problems. Students will learn how to use AI tools to accelerate coding, automate data pipelines, query and structure large datasets, clean and validate data, and develop reproducible analyses. With these skills, students will conduct industry analyses, use data to understand whether business decisions caused measurable changes in outcomes, and apply advanced demand estimation techniques to analyze consumer behavior. Throughout the course, AI will be treated not as a substitute for economic reasoning, but as a tool for scaling and improving empirical strategy work. No prior coding experience is required.
faculty_bio: Kevin R. Williams is Professor of Economics at the Yale School of Management and an affiliated faculty member of Yale’s Department of Economics. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/kevin-r-williams)) His research focuses on industrial organization and applied microeconomics, particularly pricing, retailing, product variety, and dynamic markets such as airlines. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/kevin-r-williams)) He teaches courses including Empirical Strategy Lab and Competitive Strategy, and previously served as an assistant and associate professor at Yale. ([kevinrwilliams.com](https://kevinrwilliams.com/teaching/)) Williams earned his PhD in economics from the University of Minnesota and his BA in economics and mathematics from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/kevin-r-williams))

Course Description: Most of you will spend 80% of your career as part of a team. In this highly interactive course, you will learn the theory and practice of leading, managing, and performing in task-oriented teams. Through weekly in-class exercises that simulate the challenges encountered by real-world groups and leaders, you will develop a conceptual understanding of group dynamics, experience these dynamics firsthand, and develop practical skills to support team effectiveness. You will leave with a better understanding of how to create structures and environments to help your teams make high-quality decisions, produce innovative solutions to problems, complete their projects in a timely and efficient manner, while supporting the development and experience of individual team members.
faculty_bio: David M. Munguia Gomez is an Assistant Professor of Organizational Behavior at Yale School of Management. His research examines how people allocate rewards and opportunities—such as college admission and employment—with particular attention to ethical tensions involving merit, circumstance, and disadvantage, using experiments, surveys, and interviews. He earned a PhD in behavioral science from the University of Chicago Booth School of Business and an AB in psychology from Princeton University, and his research has appeared in leading management and psychology journals and received best paper awards. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/david-m-munguia-gomez))

Course Description:
Most of the attention to issues of financial stability focuses on the role of the central bank and prudential regulators in preventing the failure of systemically important financial institutions. As we’ve learned through the experience of the Global Financial Crisis of 2008 (GFC), as well as the regional bank failures in the United States and the failure of Credit Suisse in Switzerland in the spring of 2023, preventive efforts are not always successful.
The capability of public authorities to manage the orderly failure of systemically important financial institutions, without resort to public support on an open institution basis – in other words, a bailout that protects the shareholders, creditors, and management of the institution – has been a goal of the United States and the international community since the 2008 Crisis. The failure of public authorities to have this capability increases the risk of financial crises and erodes public trust and support for preventive efforts. It also creates an unlevel playing field in favor of institutions that are deemed “too big to fail” and long-run market expectations and moral hazard that lay the groundwork for future financial system instability.
The purpose of this course is to review the work on systemic resolution that has been done, both in the United States and internationally, since the 2008 Crisis to develop the capability of public authorities to manage the orderly failure of systemically important banks, both global (GSIBs) and domestic (DSIBs). It will consider the financial stability, accountability, competition, and moral hazard trade-offs between open institution support and resolution and the difficult choices policymakers have to make.
faculty_bio: Martin Gruenberg is a Lecturer in Management at Yale School of Management and an inaugural lecturer in Yale’s Paul A. Volcker Lecture Series. His academic work focuses on financial stability, banking regulation, and policy responses to financial crises through Yale’s Program on Financial Stability. Gruenberg previously chaired the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) and held leadership roles with the International Association of Deposit Insurers, the Financial Stability Board, and the Financial Stability Oversight Council; he earned a J.D. from Case Western Reserve Law School and an A.B. from Princeton University. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/martin-gruenberg))

Course Description:
This course explores the history of finance through direct engagement with primary objects — clay tablets, coins, bonds, banknotes, securities, and artworks — held in Yale's extraordinary collections. Each week, students meet in a different Yale collection under the guidance of expert curators to examine objects that document the invention and evolution of financial instruments, institutions, and markets from antiquity to the modern era.
The course traces several interlocking themes: the emergence of debt and credit in ancient Mesopotamia; the invention and diffusion of coinage; the development of sovereign debt, corporate securities, and paper money in early-modern Europe and China; the global expansion of finance through trading companies and colonial enterprise; and the material culture of money in Africa and the Americas. By working directly with original objects, students develop a tactile understanding of financial innovation that no textbook can replicate — and confront the physical, legal, and artistic dimensions of instruments that are today entirely digital.
 
Learning Objectives
1.	Understand the deep history of financial instruments and institutions through primary material evidence
2.	Develop the ability to "read" financial objects — contracts, coins, bonds, banknotes, artworks — as sources of economic information
3.	Trace the co-evolution of financial innovation, legal institutions, and political authority across civilizations
4.	Appreciate the global diffusion of financial technology and the role of cultural exchange in shaping markets
faculty_bio: William N. Goetzmann is the Edwin J. Beinecke Professor of Finance and Management Studies and Faculty Director of the International Center for Finance at the Yale School of Management. His research examines alternative investing, factor investing, behavioral finance, financial history, and the art market, building on earlier work on stock-market predictability, hedge funds, and performance measurement. He teaches portfolio management, alternative investments, real estate, and financial history. Goetzmann holds a Ph.D. and an M.B.A. from Yale and has authored or co-authored several books on finance, investment, and financial history. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/william-n-goetzmann))
