Course Description: Students in this course will learn how to manage software development teams through the process of building a basic web application. We will discuss “agile”, continuous delivery, “devops”, and related management practices. Along the way, students will acquire elementary software development skills for creating consumer web applications including both front-end development (typically HTML, JavaScript and CSS) and back-end development (typically Google’s Go language). The coursework in MGT656 typically includes homework (mostly programming assignments completed individually), pre-class quizzes, in-class exams, and a group final project. Some experience programming is beneficial, though not necessary for the motivated student. The course is open to all Yale students. In some semesters MGT660 is offered as an advanced version of this course. For more information, see the class website at http://656.mba (offline between semesters).
faculty_bio: Kyle Jensen is the Shanna and Eric Bass ’05 Director of Entrepreneurial Programs, Associate Dean, and Professor in the Practice of Entrepreneurship at Yale School of Management. His research interests include entrepreneurship, intellectual property, and innovation, and he teaches courses on entrepreneurship, technology, and large language models. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/kyle-jensen)) An entrepreneur, developer, and engineer, Jensen previously co-founded companies including Rho AI, PriorSmart, and Agrivida, and holds a PhD from MIT and a BS from the University of Illinois. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/kyle-jensen))

Course Description: An introduction to the business corporation laws affecting the rights and roles of corporate boards of directors, senior executive officers, and shareholders, with attention to both large, publicly traded firms and to closely-held companies. Shareholders' economic interests are examined from the perspective of limited liability and dividend standards, expectations of liquidity or transferability of shares, and the use of debt capital as a mode of financing corporate activity. Shareholders' limited participation rights in corporate decision making will be examined from the perspective of state and federal rules governing shareholder voting and the disclosure of corporate information and the notion of managerial expertise (e.g., as evidenced by judicial application of the "business judgment rule"). The latter part of the course will focus on directors' and officers' fiduciary obligations to shareholders, examining the operation of these duties in a variety of settings and transactions. Issues relating to the roles and functions assumed by corporate attorneys (with respect to their clients) and the role of business corporations within society will also be addressed.  This course is cross-listed with Yale Law School. It will be held there and will follow their academic calendar.
faculty_bio: John Morley is a professor of law at Yale Law School and a faculty member affiliated with Yale School of Management. His research and teaching focus on investment funds, private equity, corporate law, and financial regulation. He is particularly known for scholarship examining the structure and governance of mutual funds, hedge funds, and other investment organizations.

Course Description: Whereas all leaders strive toward positive results – black ink on balance sheets, erected buildings, networked information systems – mission-oriented leaders strive toward humanity’s best interests and the flourishing of all creation. In this course, students will learn about how to bring together practices of discernment, social entrepreneurship, and leadership to make a vision – a transcendent ideal – become real. Mission-oriented innovators are not just dreamers. They take seriously the scope of societal challenges both locally and globally, and the finitude of resources to meet these challenges. To effect change, they must be strategic, creative, and thoughtful. They must rely on relationships with constituents and other like-minded allies, and, when people come together, they become more than the sum of their parts. This course is cross-listed with the Yale Divinity school and will follow their academic calendar.
faculty_bio: Teresa Chahine is a Senior Lecturer in Social Entrepreneurship at Yale School of Management and Faculty Director of the Social Innovation Initiative at Yale Jackson School of Global Affairs. She teaches social entrepreneurship and researches tools for advancing social and environmental determinants of health, including how to finance, measure, and scale social impact. Chahine previously launched a public-health entrepreneurship program at Harvard and founded Lebanon’s first venture-philanthropy organization. She is also the author of *Social Entrepreneurship: Building Impact Step by Step*. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/teresa-chahine))

Course Title: Innovation, Investments, and New Frontiers in Medicine
Course Description: This course serves as a description and critical assessment of the life science industries, focusing on the pharmaceutical or biopharmaceutical, but including discussion of the medical device and diagnostic industries. The topics covered include drug discovery, preclinical development, clinical investigation, and economic, financial, and strategic considerations of the drug development process. Emerging areas of interest and development, ethical issues and societal impact will also be explored. A multidisciplinary perspective is provided by the faculty, who represent clinical, life, and management sciences. Various guests from academia and industry also participate.  Prerequisite for the course is one semester of college level biology.
faculty_bio: Stephen Knight is a Lecturer in Management at Yale School of Management and President and Managing Partner of F-Prime Capital, where he invests broadly across healthcare. His professional focus includes pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies, healthcare innovation, and evaluating transformative medical technologies. Before joining F-Prime, he held senior roles in biotechnology and consulting and conducted research at AT&T Bell Laboratories, the National Institutes of Health, and Yale University. Knight holds an M.D. and M.B.A. from Yale and a summa cum laude B.S. in biology from Columbia University. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/stephen-knight))

Course Description:
In this course, we will explore how to drive growth in emerging consumer-facing ventures. Through case studies, frameworks, and practical applications, students will examine how to win the hearts and minds and open the wallets of consumers while profitably scaling through an agile, test-and-learn approach.

Key objectives:

• Understand the building blocks of a high-performing growth strategy.

• Analyze unit economics (LTV and CAC) and key drivers of profitability.

• Navigate advertising channels, media mix strategies, and measurement approaches.

• Develop creative testing and conversion optimization tactics.

• Leverage CRM tools and tactics to build customer loyalty and community.

• Create effective content and partnerships to amplify brand reach.

• Design an integrated growth campaign and define success metrics.

Students will gain actionable insights for entrepreneurial growth strategies and deeper understanding of growth marketing frameworks also applicable to larger consumer-facing enterprises.
faculty_bio: Laura Jones (LJ) Joukovski is a Lecturer in the Practice of Management at Yale School of Management, where she teaches Direct-to-Consumer Entrepreneurship. Her focus is on the practical challenges of building and scaling consumer brands, including strategy, marketing, finance, operations, and organizational leadership. She is CEO of DFTBA, a board member, investor, and advisor, and previously served as CEO of JustFab and helped scale brands including Fabletics and Savage X Fenty. Joukovski holds an MBA from Yale SOM and a BS in Economics from Davidson College. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/laura-joukovski))

Course Description: This course will provide an in-depth examination of the basic structure and purposes of secured credit transactions under Article 9 of the Uniform Commercial Code. Discussions will focus on the essential elements of secured financing (including the creation and enforcement of security interests in various types of tangible and intangible property) as well as the longstanding debate over the essential utility and fairness of contractual security devices and the secured creditor's priority. We will also consider the treatment of security interests in bankruptcy proceedings; securitizations as an alternative to traditional methods of secured lending; consignments; bailments; letters of credit; and a variety of other commercial law concepts. Prior courses in commercial transactions, corporate finance, and bankruptcy, although helpful, are not required. Relevant commercial concepts will be explained as they arise. Students should expect a lively discussion of a number of important issues of current and enduring significance in the study of commercial law. This course is cross-listed with the Law School and will follow the Law School academic calendar.

Course Description:
The purpose of this course is to provide students with an opportunity to explore being an entrepreneur by purchasing a company, rather than starting one from scratch. The readings and class discussions will help students understand how to purchase a business, finance an acquisition, and operate and grow a business. The cases and conversations will help students understand what it is like being a young, first time CEO and what types of challenges and issues will be encountered.
The general course structure will follow the lifecycle of an entrepreneur who purchases a business to operate. The first few session will explore the concept of entrepreneurship through acquisition and how this compares to different forms of entrepreneurship and its pros and cons. How to purchase a business and what type of business to purchase will be examined. How to operate and grow a business as a young, first time CEO will be considered. What happens when a business works well and when it does not work well will be discussed. Finally, how and when to sell a business and what that means for the entrepreneur and business will be reviewed. This course will require active participation in class. Please be prepared and committed to participate in class. If you do not enjoy participating in class, this might not be the right course for you. Official and unofficial auditing is not permitted. Please see the Registrar’s Office (not the instructor) for all enrollment, registration, and auditing questions.

Course Description: This survey course focuses on the policy and business logic for making environmental issues and sustainability a core focus of corporate strategy and management. Students are asked to analyze when and how sustainability leadership can translate into competitive advantage by helping to cut costs, reduce risk, drive growth, and promote brand identity and intangible value. The course seeks to provide students with an introduction to the range of sustainability issues and challenges that companies face in today’s fast-changing marketplace. It introduces key corporate sustainability terms, concepts, tools, strategies, and frameworks based on the overarching theory that the traditional profit-maximizing mission of business (often called shareholder primacy) is giving way to a new vision of stakeholder responsibility that still seeks to provide good returns to the enterprise’s owners but also acknowledges obligations to employees, suppliers, customers, communities, and society more broadly. The course combines lectures, case studies, and class discussions on management theory and tools, the legal and regulatory frameworks that shape the business-environment interface, and the evolving role of business in society. It explores how to deal with a world of diverse stakeholders, increasing transparency, and rising expectations related to corporate environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance. Self-scheduled examination. This course is cross-listed with the School of Environment and will follow the YSE academic calendar. *Note*: A first (extra) class session on Tuesday, September 1, 2026, from 4:00 - 5:30 pm in the Burke Auditorium of Kroon Hall at 195 Prospect Street. This class is optional but encouraged.

Esty is the Hillhouse Professor of Environmental Law and Policy and a Professor of Management at Yale, with appointments spanning Yale Law School, the School of Management, and the School of the Environment. His research and teaching focus on environmental law and policy, sustainability, climate change, and environmental governance. He previously served as Commissioner of Connecticut’s Department of Energy and Environmental Protection and held senior roles at the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Course Description: The capability and scale of modern AI applications is now something that we have to reckon with constantly. This class invites you to set aside dedicated time to focus on the study of the technology behind the news. We develop theoretical intuition and practical skills side by side. The central practice for this class is to use AI coding agents to study the subject of AI, which serves as a template for continued learning in this new age. We work through machine learning fundamentals and deep learning neural networks, language models and GenAI, extending to agentic AI and real-word use. Workshops and homework assignments introduce critical thinking frameworks for working with AI as a learning tutor and thinking partner, and for building AI applications. The class is designed for students who have at least introductory STEM background in either coding or math, as well as solid communication skills and the self-drive for craftsmanship. This course is cross-listed with Computer Science and will follow the Yale College academic calendar.

Challenges and threats of globalization: inclusion and inequality, emerging global players, global governance, climate change, and nuclear weapons proliferation. This course meets at the Jackson School and follows their academic calendar. This class is cross-listed with the Jackson School of Global Affairs and follows their academic calendar. Prerequisite: background in international economics and data analysis. Preference to seniors majoring in Economics or EP&E.

Forman is a professor of diagnostic radiology, economics, public health, and management at Yale, where he directs the MD/MBA program and the healthcare focus area of the MBA for Executives program. Course Description: A crisis can strike at any time, and it can have major impacts on a business, its reputation, and its customers. This course prepares future industry leaders to navigate crises. Each session dives into real-world case studies encompassing data breaches, product failures, regulatory incidents, service disruptions, cybersecurity attacks, and more. Through in-depth analysis and practical applications, students explore the multifaceted landscape of tech crises, crafting actionable crisis management plans. This course arms participants with a comprehensive playbook, honing their abilities to mitigate risks, lead during crises, and learn from incidents, ensuring preparedness and resilience in the ever-evolving tech sphere.
faculty_bio: Kathryn Guarini is a Lecturer in the Practice of Management at Yale School of Management and a Senior Fellow at Yale Engineering. She teaches and consults on technology, innovation, leadership, and crisis management in the technology industry. Her background includes serving as IBM’s global Chief Information Officer from 2021 to 2023, COO of IBM Research, and a research career in semiconductor technology. She holds a PhD and MS from Stanford University and a BS from Yale University, all in applied physics, and is a named inventor on more than 65 U.S. patents. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/kathryn-guarini))

Course Title: Large language models: technology and applications
Course Description: MGT 802 introduces students to the internal workings of large language models. The course begins with the basics of neural networks and progresses through recurrent neural networks, embeddings, transformers, training, and architectural alternatives (e.g. attention variants, mixture-of-experts models, and state space models). Each class session has three components: an on-paper quiz based on pre-class reading, a lecture, and a hands-on coding activity. The course concludes with an in-class final exam. Students who complete the course should be well prepared for employment in frontier AI labs or, at minimum, somewhat better equipped to survive the singularity.

Course Description:
Fixed income markets are among the largest in the world and fixed income products are a key component of any
investment strategy. This course covers the valuation and risk management of the key fixed income products –
bonds, futures, forwards, and swaps. It combines theory with practical examples demonstrating the complications
that arise when applying theory to realistic situations.

This course sets the foundation for options, derivatives, structured products and financial engineering covered in
MGT 900 (Fall-2 2026) and MGT 901 (Spring-2 2027).
faculty_bio: Saman Majd is a Lecturer in Management at Yale School of Management. His teaching focuses on fixed-income markets, derivatives, and related financial instruments, including an advanced fixed-income markets course he taught at MIT Sloan. Before returning to academia, he held senior roles at Deutsche Asset Management and Salomon Brothers, including global leadership of derivatives and fixed-income government-bond trading. He previously taught finance at Wharton and Yale and holds a PhD and SM from MIT Sloan and a BA from Oxford. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/saman-majd))

Course Description:
Artificial Intelligence  is a transformative force across the financial services industry, reshaping both traditional finance firms and the fast-growing fintech landscape. Its applications grow rapidly from fraud detection, algorithmic trading to AI-based personalized financial advisory, and risk management, enhancing operational efficiency, accuracy, and strategic competitiveness.

Unlike past technologies, AI (particularly the latest generation of Generative and Agentic Models) impacts the core of financial business models. It is driving a shift from traditional finance firms toward fully digital, AI-driven providers, with far-reaching implications for business models, workforce dynamics, and the future of finance careers..

This course explores the innovative application of AI in the financial sector, focusing on the technological foundations and strategic use cases shaping its future. It examines the key challenges and opportunities in developing and deploying next-generation AI solutions, including both intrapreneurial initiatives within existing firms and new venture creation. Each week covers a core AI-in-finance topic, integrating business impact with technical depth, while addressing regulatory and business considerations.
faculty_bio: Eren Kurshan is a Lecturer in Management at Yale School of Management. An AI researcher and technology executive, Kurshan focuses on building large-scale industrial AI systems. Their academic background includes a PhD and an M.Sc. from the University of California. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/eren-kurshan))

Course Title: Analytics in the Age of AI
Course Description:
In today’s AI-driven organizations, the real advantage isn’t just knowing how to use tools -- it’s knowing how to structure decisions. This course teaches you how to translate messy business problems into clear objectives, constraints, and tradeoffs that can be rigorously evaluated. Rather than focusing primarily on predictive modeling, we focus on deciding what to do: allocating resources, designing operations, and stress-testing strategy under uncertainty. You’ll build hands-on decision models using spreadsheet, optimization, simulation, and coding-based tools, but the real skill you’ll gain is structured thinking that applies across consulting, product, operations, and entrepreneurship.

In the first half of the course, we will review and extend quantitative tools surveyed in the MBA core course MGT 405, greatly expanding the range of business problems that can be solved using existing methods. In the second half of the course, we will introduce simulation modeling, a useful tool for guiding decisions under uncertainty. Modeling concepts covered include linear programming, network optimization, integer programming, nonlinear optimization methods, Monte Carlo simulation, estimating summary statistics using simulation, and evaluating accuracy and precision in simulation models.

The first half of the course will be taught primarily in Excel with the Solver Add-In. The second half of the course will use R and/or Python as modeling environments, with emphasis on understanding, adapting, validating, and communicating model-based analysis rather than on prior programming experience. We will also examine how AI tools can support analytics workflows, including code generation, debugging, documentation, and model critique, while emphasizing the human judgment required to verify assumptions, interpret results, and make defensible business decisions.

There are no prerequisites for this course; you do not need to be familiar with coding to take this course.
faculty_bio: Zhen Lian is an Assistant Professor of Operations Management at Yale School of Management and a faculty fellow at Yale’s Center for Algorithms, Data, and Market Design. Her research focuses on optimization, transportation, public policy, and online marketplaces, particularly ridesharing and the gig economy. She teaches Operations Engine and Advanced Business Analytics, and previously worked as a postdoctoral fellow at Lyft on driver pay and incentive design. Lian holds a PhD from Cornell University and bachelor’s degrees from Peking University; she also helped redesign San Francisco school schedules, generating substantial transportation-cost savings. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/zhen-lian))

Todd Cort is a Senior Lecturer in Sustainability at Yale School of Management and a faculty co-director of the Yale Center for Business and the Environment at Yale. His teaching and research focus on sustainable finance, ESG, corporate sustainability, and climate-related risk. He also brings experience advising organizations on sustainability strategy, performance, and reporting. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty/todd-cort))

Course Description: This course is designed to give you the tools to identify, understand, and evaluate tax planning opportunities. To maximize the lasting benefit you will get from this course, we begin by developing a conceptual framework for thinking about how tax rules affect business decisions. Once developed, the framework is brought to life by application to a variety of settings of particular interest to MBA students (e.g., investment, compensation planning, mergers and acquisitions). This course is helpful for students who plan to: 1. Work on Wall Street (e.g., Mergers & Acquisitions); 2. Do business consulting; 3. Do corporate tax planning; 4. Have some taxation knowledge.
faculty_bio: X. Frank Zhang is the James L. Frank ’32 Professor of Accounting at Yale School of Management and has served on the Yale faculty since 2005. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/x-frank-zhang)) His research examines empirical capital markets, including stock anomalies, fundamental analysis, investor and analyst behavior, management incentives, and corporate financial reporting, using both rational and behavioral perspectives. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/x-frank-zhang)) He teaches in Yale SOM’s M.B.A., Executive M.B.A., and Ph.D. programs. ([news.yale.edu](https://news.yale.edu/2024/09/12/frank-zhang-named-james-l-frank-32-professor-accounting)) Zhang holds a Ph.D. and M.B.A. from the University of Chicago, an M.S. in Economics from Peking University, and a B.S. in Economics from Nankai University, and previously worked at Allianz Global Investors and the Bank of China. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/sites/default/files/2024-07/Frank_Zhang_CV.pdf))

Course Description:
This course examines the role of financial statement analysis in evaluating a firm’s financial performance and predicting its future economic condition. Topics include fundamental analysis and applications in both credit and equity markets. The course integrates accounting and finance into a practical framework for equity valuation, with particular emphasis on implications for IPOs, mergers and acquisitions, and equity investing. The course is designed to provide:
• Exposure to public sources of financial information used by capital market participants.
• Skills to critically analyze financial statements, SEC filings, and other disclosures.
• Insights into common accounting practices and potential earnings management techniques.
• Skills to assess and forecast a firm’s future economic condition.
• Experience applying financial information to a range of trading strategies.
faculty_bio: X. Frank Zhang is the James L. Frank ’32 Professor of Accounting at Yale School of Management and has served on the Yale faculty since 2005. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/x-frank-zhang)) His research examines empirical capital markets, including stock anomalies, fundamental analysis, investor and analyst behavior, management incentives, and corporate financial reporting, using both rational and behavioral perspectives. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/x-frank-zhang)) He teaches in Yale SOM’s M.B.A., Executive M.B.A., and Ph.D. programs. ([news.yale.edu](https://news.yale.edu/2024/09/12/frank-zhang-named-james-l-frank-32-professor-accounting)) Zhang holds a Ph.D. and M.B.A. from the University of Chicago, an M.S. in Economics from Peking University, and a B.S. in Economics from Nankai University, and previously worked at Allianz Global Investors and the Bank of China. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/sites/default/files/2024-07/Frank_Zhang_CV.pdf))

Course Title: The Private Firm CFO: Accounting and Finance Strategies
Course Description: This course equips students with the core set of tools and strategies related to accounting and financial reporting from the perspective of a Chief Financial Officer at a private, entrepreneurial company. The class focus is on accounting-related financial metrics, financial reporting, and managerial accounting, with an emphasis on structuring accounting systems from the start-up phase through to exit. Students will gain a deep understanding of compliance with GAAP, tax considerations, and performance evaluation using accounting data. The course is based on the institutional setting that applies in the United States for both the entrepreneurial firm and key private capital market providers (private equity, venture capital, and angel investors).
faculty_bio: John Manuel Barrios is an Associate Professor of Accounting at Yale School of Management and a Faculty Research Fellow at the National Bureau of Economic Research. His research spans accounting, labor economics, entrepreneurship, political economy, and antitrust, with a focus on how accounting information and regulation shape firms, workers, and markets. He teaches Financial Accounting and Valuation and The Private Firm CFO. Before joining Yale, he taught at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business and Washington University in St. Louis; he holds a Ph.D. from the University of Miami and a B.S. from Cornell University. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/john-manuel-barrios))

Course Description: How can you predict the fraction of games a baseball team will win from the number of runs scored for and against? When does it make sense to try for a two point conversion in football? What are good picks for a March Madness basketball pool? In Mathletics, we will tackle (!) sports questions like these using probability models, statistics, decision analysis, and spreadsheets. The goal is to further develop your modeling skills while having fun with examples from the wonderful world of sports. Prerequisites: MGT 403 (Probability Modeling and Statistics), MGT 405 (Modeling Managerial Decisions); S&DS 2300 or an equivalent course/background; Proficiency in a programming language (e.g., Python, R, C++).
faculty_bio: Tobias J. Moskowitz is the Theodore O. Yntema Professor of Finance at Yale School of Management and a research associate at the National Bureau of Economic Research. His research focuses on empirical asset pricing, behavioral finance, and the economics of sports, and he teaches finance and investment-related courses. He previously held a faculty position at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business and is recognized for influential work on investment behavior and financial markets. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/tobias-moskowitz))

Course Title: Risk, Insurance and Finance for Households and Small Enterprises
Course Description: Around the world, households and the small enterprises they run (the self-employed, family businesses, gig workers, smallholder farmers) face significant risks to their incomes, as well as challenges in growing them. Insurance, credit and other financial services are designed to address these issues, but in many cases the markets for these instruments may be incomplete or missing, particularly for the least well-off or in marginalized communities. This course studies the nature of risk and the demand for financial services among households and small enterprises in both developed and developing economies; the role of financial instruments in addressing those needs; the reasons why these markets may fail; and potential solutions, from market design to public policy. Throughout, we pay attention to the different forms these instruments may take and the different potential providers, including the commercial market, informal institutions, social arrangements, nonprofits and the state. The emphasis will be on the household and small enterprise as a single economic unit (how ordinary people manage everyday risk and finance their livelihoods, including access to capital for starting or growing a small business) rather than on personal financial planning, the financing of large or high-growth ventures, corporate hedging or system-level finance. Throughout, we will draw on economic theory and empirical evidence.
faculty_bio: Robert T. Jensen is a Professor of Economics at the Yale School of Management and previously served as a professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania. His research focuses on poverty and economic development, particularly gender, health, education, fertility, and the role of markets and private enterprise. He has conducted research in China, the Dominican Republic, Mexico, Nepal, and India, and holds a PhD from Princeton University. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/robert-t-jensen))

Course Description: This course provides an introduction to the study of International Trade. The goal of the course is to teach you a set of conceptual tools that are useful for understanding what determines international trade and foreign investments. We will first review international trade theories that try to explain: Why do countries trade with each other? Do countries gain from trade? Who are the winners and losers? What goods should countries import and export? Can existing trade theories explain the rapid growth of China? Second, we will focus on foreign direct investment, multinational firms, and business opportunities in developing countries. For instance, we will explore what are the benefits and costs of hosting multinational companies in the developing world, both in the short- and long-run (in terms of productivity, living standards, culture, environmental effects). Third, we will analyze the role of trade policy. We will try to learn what are the trade and welfare effects of trade policy. This part of the course will review recent research that evaluates the effects of the trade war between China and the U.S. The course is self-contained. However, a background in micro and macroeconomics is desirable. For SOM students, the core is sufficient. You will get more out of the class if you often read the business section of a major newspaper (NYT, WDJ, FT, Economist, etc.).
faculty_bio: Diana Van Patten is an Assistant Professor of Economics at Yale School of Management. Her research focuses on economic development, international trade, economic history, and the effects of foreign direct investment and trade in developing countries. She earned a PhD in Economics from UCLA in 2020 and previously was a postdoctoral associate at Princeton University’s International Economics Section. Originally from Costa Rica, she also holds a BSc from the Universidad de Costa Rica. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/diana-van-patten))

Course Description:
The purpose of this class is to teach you how to evaluate public policies. This will help you:
a) Understand what political viewpoints are most reasonable in light of the existing evidence
b) Constructively discuss public policy

The course will emphasize two perspectives:
1) Cost-benefit analysis – how can we quantitatively determine the costs and benefits of a given policy by determining who is impacted and valuing those impacts?
2) Economic theory – when do markets work well? When might public provision be better?

Questions covered will include (among others):
Public transit systems help people travel more quickly, but they cost a lot of money. How should we evaluate if this cost if worthwhile?
A carbon tax would harm consumers today by making goods more expensive; this burden would be highest for low-income households who spend a larger percentage of income on emission-intensive goods. It would also reduce carbon emissions and combat global warming. Should we do it?
Most OECD countries have publicly provided healthcare. In Medicare Parts C/D and the Affordable Care Act, the US is moving increasingly towards a system of privately provided care with government subsidies. Should people under the age of 65 be allowed to buy into Medicare?
Should we have school vouchers which allow parents to use public funding to choose amongst local and non-local public schools, as well as private or charter schools?
Unemployment insurance provides an income stream for people who lose their job. But evidence shows that people find work faster when unemployment insurance is less generous. How generous should UI be?
Should we replace the social safety net with a system in which every single person receives $12,000 in cash whether or not they are currently working?
Should we replace the current social security program with individual savings accounts?
What is the role of AI in public policy?
faculty_bio: Jason Abaluck is a Professor of Economics and Management at Yale University and a faculty member of Yale School of Management. His research and teaching focus on health economics, behavioral economics, public policy, and the design of markets and government programs. He is also a faculty research fellow at the National Bureau of Economic Research and received the 2024 John Bates Clark Medal for his contributions to economics. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/jason-abaluck))

Course Description:
The art market is highly seductive, with its multibillion-dollar industry, hyped NFTs, sensational auctions, wealthy collectors, and lavish vernissages. Yet the reality is challenging. Nearly 30% of galleries operate at a loss, and over 90% of artists cannot make a living from their work. How can entrepreneurs succeed? Why does Gagosian generate over $1 billion in sales while the average gallery turns over only $200,000? What impact will Web3 have? Can new models replace auction houses and art fairs?
This course offers students firsthand insights into the art market through theoretical analysis and conversations with leading practitioners. Past speakers have included Jeff Koons, Jerry Saltz, Cecilia Alemani, and Noah Horowitz (CEO of Art Basel). Students will shape these sessions, challenge the experts, and develop their own perspectives. Fifteen places are reserved for artists from the Yale School of Art, creating a uniquely diverse and enriching classroom experience.
faculty_bio: Magnus Resch is a Lecturer in Management at Yale School of Management, where he has taught since 2019. His research and teaching focus on the intersection of art, technology, and business, including the economics and entrepreneurship of the art market. He is an art-market expert, serial entrepreneur, and bestselling author of books including *How to Collect Art* and *How to Become a Successful Artist*. Resch holds a PhD in economics and has studied at Harvard, the London School of Economics, and the University of St. Gallen. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/magnus-resch))

Course Description: One day, you’ll lead something—perhaps a team, a company, or an enterprise entirely your own. When that day comes, every decision you make about people, policy, capital, or organizational culture will reflect deeper beliefs about what really matters. This course helps you understand and test those beliefs. Is the goal to maximize economic value? To create value for all stakeholders? Balance purpose and profit? Build something that endures? Or something else entirely? Your own thoughts about such beliefs will be stretched and challenged as complexity builds throughout the course—short-term demands against longer time horizons, competing interests and pressures, unexpected developments. Through direct conversations with CEOs and real-world examples, we’ll examine and debate how leaders navigate these complexities, and what they rely on to guide decisions and build enduring organizations. Ultimately, you’ll form your own view of what you're optimizing for when you're in charge.
faculty_bio: Jon Iwata is a Lecturer in the Practice of Management and Executive Director of Yale SOM’s Program on Stakeholder Innovation and Management. His work focuses on stakeholder capitalism, organizational leadership, corporate purpose, and responsible business practices, and he contributes to Yale teaching and research on these topics. Before joining Yale, Iwata spent more than 35 years at IBM, where he served in senior leadership roles including Senior Vice President and Chief Brand Officer. He holds a bachelor’s degree from San Jose State University. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/jon-iwata))

Course Description:
Due to the hands-on nature of this course, we strictly require class attendance and participation. This course is a highly practical course that puts students in the seat of the private equity investor evaluating a live investment opportunity. It is co-instructed by Professor Song Ma, Professor of Finance and Entrepreneurship, and Mr. James Soldano, Managing Partner, Sterling Investment Partners.

Working in 4–5 person deal teams, students follow a single transaction from initial due diligence through final bid, learning to assess an opportunity through business, commercial, and financial due diligence; negotiate and structure the financing; design performance-oriented management incentives; negotiate a purchase agreement; and present a fully vetted recommendation—with a proposed valuation—to an investment committee composed of the instructors and TAs. Weekly lectures reinforce each stage of the deal lifecycle, culminating in a team IC presentation.

Alongside the deal itself, students will learn how to leverage AI to enhance the efficiency and quality of due diligence, “stress test” an investment thesis and financial modeling assumptions, and to review legal agreements, including credit term sheets and the purchase agreement. The goal is not just to evaluate a deal but to learn how AI is reshaping the private equity investor's workflow. 
Prerequisites: MBA students must have earned at least a PR grade in both Investor and Sourcing and Managing Funds. Students enrolled in other programs must demonstrate proficiency in equivalent coursework covering both investments and corporate finance.
faculty_bio: Song Ma is a Professor of Finance and Entrepreneurship at Yale School of Management, a Faculty Research Fellow at the National Bureau of Economic Research, and an affiliated faculty member at Yale Law School’s Center for the Study of Corporate Law and Yale SOM’s Program on Entrepreneurship. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/song-ma)) His research focuses on innovation economics, entrepreneurship, financial economics, artificial intelligence, and big data, with additional work in corporate strategy, antitrust, labor, and business law. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/song-ma)) He teaches courses including Entrepreneurial Finance, Venture Capital and Private Equity, and Finance and Society, and joined Yale SOM’s faculty in 2016. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/song-ma)) Ma earned a PhD in Finance from Duke University in 2016 and a BA in Economics from Zhejiang University in 2010. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/song-ma))

Course Description: This course focuses on the investment decision process of leveraged buyout (LBO) firms. Students will gain an understanding of how private equity professionals evaluate opportunities and manage due diligence. Topics covered include early deal screening, thesis/risk assessment, due diligence, business forecasting and LBO modeling, debt structure alternatives, and value creation strategies. Classes will be comprised of discussions of organizational frameworks and practices of PE firms, and group analysis of LBO transactions. Student teams will prepare investment materials based on transaction case studies which mirror a PE firm’s process of evaluating LBO opportunities.
faculty_bio: Joshua Cascade is a Lecturer in the Practice of Management at Yale School of Management. His teaching focuses on private equity, including leveraged buyout transactions, which he has taught to MBA students at Yale since 2018. Cascade is a private equity investor with more than 25 years of industry experience and has led or co-led buyouts totaling more than $2 billion in acquisition value. He was formerly a Managing Partner at Wellspring Capital, previously worked at Odyssey Investment Partners and The Blackstone Group, and earned a BBA from the University of Michigan in 1994. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/joshua-cascade))

K. Sudhir is the James L. Frank ’32 Professor of Marketing, Private Enterprise, and Management at Yale School of Management and serves as faculty director of Yale’s China India Consumer Insights Program. His research and teaching focus on quantitative marketing, including customer analytics, pricing, innovation, and digital markets. He is known for applying econometric and statistical methods to important problems in marketing and consumer behavior. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/k-sudhir))

Course Title: Money, Power, and Purpose: Philanthropy in a Changing World (formerly Modern Philanthropy)
Course Description: Co-taught by a philanthropic advisor and an economics faculty member, this course (formerly called Modern Philanthropy) will examine alternative approaches to philanthropy and address many of the challenges and tradeoffs facing modern philanthropists. The main audience for the course includes students who aspire to be philanthropic advisors, program officers in a foundation or social venture firm, or who wish to be productive philanthropists themselves. The course will also be useful for students who aspire to work in development or lead a nonprofit organization. We will examine the history of philanthropy and foundations, the current state of philanthropy, debates about the role of philanthropy in society, and the complicated relationship between philanthropy and social justice. We will debate the tradeoffs between different approaches to organizing and designing philanthropic activities—for example perpetual foundations, sunsetting foundations, and social impact investing. We will examine different approaches that philanthropic organizations take in deciding how and where to give money including the “strategic philanthropy” and “effective altruism” paradigms and examine different approaches to evaluating grantees and grantee outcomes.
faculty_bio: Paige MacLean is a Lecturer in the Practice of Management at Yale School of Management and a fellow at Yale’s Program on Social Enterprise, Innovation, and Impact. She teaches philanthropy, focusing on high-impact approaches and drawing practitioners into discussions of current issues and case studies. She also advises the Social Impact Consulting Club and Golub Capital Board Fellows Program. Her background includes more than 20 years in organizational and board leadership, strategy consulting, fundraising, and nonprofit development, including work at Boston Consulting Group and Wellspring Consulting. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/paige-maclean))

Course Description: This course is designed to explore the ever-increasing impact of technology on our lives—as individuals, consumers, employees, managers, and policymakers. Technology has profoundly reshaped how we access information, interact with others, experience the world, and make decisions. Rather than focusing on the technical features of emerging tools, including, yes, Artificial Intelligence, the course examines the psychological and behavioral consequences of living in a technology-saturated environment. By developing an evidence-based and nuanced understanding of these issues, this course will enable more effective usage and management of technology.
faculty_bio: Gal Zauberman is the Joseph F. Cullman 3rd Professor of Marketing at Yale School of Management. His research examines consumer judgment and decision-making, time perception, financial decision-making, the nature of experiences, and memory for emotions and choice. He earned a PhD from Duke University’s Fuqua School of Business in 2000 and a BA from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill in 1994, and has received several research awards, including the Early Career Award for Distinguished Contributions to Consumer Psychology. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/gal-zauberman))

Course Description: This course builds on MGT 402 (Basics of Accounting) and provides students with the skills to better understand financial statements; the focus is on "why", not just "what". The course focuses on the application of accounting concepts and contains numerous examples from the real world on financial statement reporting. The goal of the course is to recognize each transaction's underlying economics, understand the relevant accounting rules, and how they impact managers’ decision-making. This course will be helpful for students who plan to use company financial statements in their careers or those who want to improve their understanding of financial accounting.
faculty_bio: Aneesh Raghunandan is an Associate Professor of Accounting at Yale School of Management, having previously been an assistant professor of accounting at the London School of Economics. His research examines environmental, social, and governance issues, firms’ political and economic connections to governments, corporate irresponsibility, and the reporting and consequences of corporate subsidies. He holds a PhD from Stanford Graduate School of Business and undergraduate degrees from Yale University, and he worked at the Federal Reserve between his undergraduate and graduate studies. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/aneesh-raghunandan))

Course Title: Sales and Negotiation: Figure Out the Other Side
Course Description: Through weekly practice cases, students will learn to lead more persuasive conversations and craft smarter deals—whether pitching to investors, managing clients, or navigating difficult conversations with friends and family. New for 2025, this update of Dr. Cain’s popular negotiation elective introduces a growing emphasis on sales, featuring guest insights from leading experts in the field. (Best for students who haven’t taken MGT 887 or other negotiation electives with Prof. Cain.)
faculty_bio: Daylian Cain is a Senior Lecturer in Negotiations, Leadership, and Ethics at Yale School of Management. His research focuses on judgment and decision-making, behavioral business ethics, conflicts of interest, and altruism, while his teaching emphasizes negotiation, sales, and leadership. Before joining Yale in 2007, he was a Russell Sage Fellow in Behavioral Economics at Harvard; he is originally from Nova Scotia, has won national teaching awards, and has appeared on National Geographic’s *Brain Games*. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/daylian-cain))

Course Description: Negotiating a job offer, founding a startup, resolving a dispute with a boss or coworker (or significant other) – negotiation skills will help you navigate all of these situations. This half-semester elective will hone your negotiation skills so that you can better negotiate with managers, investors, clients, coworkers, friends, and family. Each class session you will participate in real negotiation exercises with your peers. These exercises – paired with lectures, written reflections, and small group activities – will help you build a “toolkit” of negotiations skills and strategies that will make you more effective at creating and claiming value in your professional and personal life. This class covers both introductory and advanced topics; it assumes no prior experience with negotiation. Non-SOM students are welcome to enroll in the course.
faculty_bio: Erin L. Frey is an Assistant Professor of Organizational Behavior at Yale School of Management. Her research examines failure, recovery, and second chances, including how individuals, groups, and industries respond to setbacks and seek rehabilitation across contexts such as the military, scientific organizations, entertainment, and white-collar crime. She earned her PhD from Harvard Business School, completed a postdoctoral fellowship at the University of Virginia, and previously served as an assistant professor at the University of Southern California. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/erin-l-frey))

Course Description: “It’s all about who you know.” From this familiar phrase, it seems intuitively clear that successful management of social networks is critical. Unfortunately, our intuition often does not take us far beyond this basic idea, and as a result, networks can impede—rather than facilitate—the realization of our goals. Thus, this course has two central goals: (1) to identify what kinds of networks facilitate personal and organizational success, and (2) to understand when we can (and cannot) achieve valuable ties that provide such strategic advantages. Students will be expected to actively participate in class discussions, especially those involving real-world cases that highlight both the value and limitations of social networks. Assessment is based on individual reflection memos and a final group project. Interested non-SOM students may contact the instructor and attend the first day of class.
faculty_bio: Minjae Kim is an Assistant Professor of Organizational Behavior at Yale School of Management. His research examines when, why, and how social actors coordinate their actions, with applications to organizations, entrepreneurship, politics, and cultural markets. His projects explore elite closure, founder influence on employee retention, and how low-status projects can succeed in cultural markets. Before joining Yale, he taught at Rice University, was a postdoctoral fellow at Northwestern University, earned his PhD from MIT Sloan, and worked as a consultant for local governments. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/minjae-kim))

Course Description: This course surveys the causes, events, policy responses, and aftermath of the recent global financial crisis. The main goal is to provide a comprehensive view of this major economic event within a framework that explains the dynamics of financial crises in a modern economy. Comprehensive survey of the causes, events, policy responses, and aftermath of the global financial crisis of 2007-09. Study of the dynamics of financial crises in a modern economy. The course uses a "flipped" classroom for most meetings, with students watching lectures before class, posting questions and discussion online, and continuing those discussions in the classroom. Course requirements include in-class quizzes and an in-person final exam. Prerequisite: Successful completion of a course in introductory economics. The course is cross-listed at SOM, Yale Law School, and Yale College, but is open to all Yale students. Students enrolled outside of those schools should consult their registrar for details on receiving credit.
faculty_bio: Andrew Metrick is the Janet L. Yellen Professor of Finance and Management at Yale School of Management and serves as faculty director of the Yale Program on Financial Stability. His research and teaching focus on financial economics, including corporate finance, financial institutions, banking, and financial crises. Before joining Yale, he was a faculty member at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/andrew-metrick))

Course Description: This half semester course will provide an introduction to real estate development, investment, finance and strategy outside of the United States.  Global investment in financial assets, the need for risk diversification, the increased accuracy of property records, greater transparency, more relaxed laws permitting foreign investment, and population movement around the world—all of these trends have led to a tremendous increase in cross-border real estate investing for both private equity and public companies.  While many studies of international real estate focus on the role of foreign real property in the U. S. institutional portfolio, this course will take a wider and more historical view of the cultural attitudes towards real estate around the world and how they impact the quality and risk of investment assets.  Detailed analysis will begin with property level due diligence in order to provide a fundamental understanding of how and why property markets differ by country beyond simple supply/demand dynamics.  This course will consist of three parts:  a.) a micro-market analysis of real property characteristics in various countries around the world, including financing, leasing and valuation; b.) an analysis of investment vehicles—public and private—available to institutional investors, as well as cross-border transactions, and c.) a macro-market view of world space and capital  markets, the rationale for international investing, trends in capital flows and portfolio composition and the various ways in which risk is measured and mitigated.  Each part of the course will require a brief individual assignment completed over a two-week period.  The first research project will be a study of a significant real property asset outside of the United States, including its market, ownership, legal structure, valuation, and transaction history.  Both the G-8 and G-20 nations will be the object of study, but individual students are free to concentrate on any country of interest.  The second research project will consist of an analysis of a private equity or publicly-traded foreign property company, its current fair value, competitive advantage and future prospects.  An interview with a top executive of a company will be encouraged and facilitated.  The third research project will consist of a comparative analysis of world property markets and the hypothetical investment in a portfolio of real estate assets across three or more foreign property markets.  The course will consist of lectures, discussion, case studies and readings on international real estate from a variety of sources.  No final exam or group project will be required.
faculty_bio: Kevin D. Gray is a Lecturer in the Practice of Management at Yale University and principal of Kevin D. Gray Consulting, a real estate advisory firm. He teaches real estate finance and investment, international real estate, and the history of real estate patronage and ownership. Gray is also co-founder of Stone Road Capital, a Bangladesh-based advisory firm focused on raising capital for real estate and infrastructure projects in Asia. His background includes real estate investment banking at PricewaterhouseCoopers Securities, an M.Arch. from the University of Pennsylvania, and an MBA from Yale SOM. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/kevin-d-gray))

Course Description:
The course is designed to introduce the challenges and pitfalls of financing new enterprises. The course primarily takes the perspective of an entrepreneur. Broadly speaking, entrepreneurial financing decisions have a life cycle. The cycle begins with identifying opportunities, moves to marshaling resources to take advantage of these opportunities and executing the business plan, and ends with harvesting the venture's success. Accordingly, the course has three sections: Identifying and Valuing Opportunities, Structuring Deals, and Harvesting Opportunities.

Increasingly, the entrepreneur does not work alone. This course pays particular attention to how artificial intelligence and autonomous agents are reshaping the way founders raise, structure, and manage capital across this life cycle. We consider how a founder might delegate to specialized agents—a market-and-opportunity scout, a valuation and modeling analyst, a deal-structuring and term-sheet advisor, an investor-relations coordinator—and what the founder must still own: judgment, relationships, and the strategic decisions that cannot be automated away.

This course combines lectures and case studies. The lecture part will equip students with important techniques in each stage of entrepreneurial finance, as well as the skills to deploy and supervise the AI tools and agents that apply these techniques at speed and scale. Those techniques are applied to case studies covering interesting entrepreneurial areas such as IT, healthcare, the sharing economy, and impact investment, with attention to how an agent-augmented founder would approach each situation differently from a traditional one.
faculty_bio: Song Ma is a Professor of Finance and Entrepreneurship at Yale School of Management, a Faculty Research Fellow at the National Bureau of Economic Research, and an affiliated faculty member at Yale Law School’s Center for the Study of Corporate Law and Yale SOM’s Program on Entrepreneurship. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/song-ma)) His research focuses on innovation economics, entrepreneurship, financial economics, artificial intelligence, and big data, with additional work in corporate strategy, antitrust, labor, and business law. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/song-ma)) He teaches courses including Entrepreneurial Finance, Venture Capital and Private Equity, and Finance and Society, and joined Yale SOM’s faculty in 2016. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/song-ma)) Ma earned a PhD in Finance from Duke University in 2016 and a BA in Economics from Zhejiang University in 2010. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/song-ma))

Course Title: Derivative Securities: Options, Futures, and Structured Products
Course Description:
Derivative securities are key components of structured products and financial engineering. This course builds on the
material in MGT 805 and covers the valuation and risk management of the basic tools of financial engineering –
forward contracts, futures, and options. The standard Black-Scholes-Merton methodology will be explored in some
depth and extensions of the model will be discussed. Financial engineering examples will be discussed throughout,
and assignments will include case studies.

Although MGT 805 is not a strict pre-requisite for this course, it is highly recommended. Students who haven’t
taken MGT 805 can take MGT 900 with the instructor’s permission.

MGT 900 is not a strict prerequisite for MGT 901 Financial Engineering (Spring-2 2027), but students who haven’t
taken MGT 900 will need the instructor’s permission to register for MGT 901.

Course requirements include regular attendance and class participation in lectures, weekly homework assignments,
an in-class midterm quiz, and a final exam. Weekly review sessions to cover homework are optional but
recommended.
faculty_bio: Saman Majd is a Lecturer in Management at Yale School of Management. His teaching focuses on fixed-income markets, derivatives, and related financial instruments, including an advanced fixed-income markets course he taught at MIT Sloan. Before returning to academia, he held senior roles at Deutsche Asset Management and Salomon Brothers, including global leadership of derivatives and fixed-income government-bond trading. He previously taught finance at Wharton and Yale and holds a PhD and SM from MIT Sloan and a BA from Oxford. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/saman-majd))

Course Description: AM required. This course is for Asset Management students only (students are pre-registered). Six to eight talks per year by leaders in the field of asset management. Potential topics include the following: client relations, cryptocurrencies, data technology, discretionary macro, real assets, risk management, short selling, and venture capital.
faculty_bio: Tobias J. Moskowitz is the Theodore O. Yntema Professor of Finance at Yale School of Management and a research associate at the National Bureau of Economic Research. His research focuses on empirical asset pricing, behavioral finance, and the economics of sports, and he teaches finance and investment-related courses. He previously held a faculty position at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business and is recognized for influential work on investment behavior and financial markets. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/tobias-moskowitz))

Course Description:
This course develops the theoretical foundations and economic intuition of modern asset pricing, organized around a
single unifying idea: the stochastic discount factor (SDF). Beginning with preferences, expected utility, and portfolio
choice, we show how the law of one price and the absence of arbitrage lead to a fundamental pricing relation, and how
essentially every asset pricing model amounts to a different theory of the discount factor. Within this framework we
treat state prices, complete and incomplete markets, and risk-neutral pricing, and we revisit the classic mean–variance
and CAPM results as special cases rather than as starting points. We then turn to consumption-based and equilibrium
models that tie risk premia to the macroeconomy, along with the risk-sharing and Pareto-optimality ideas behind them.
Throughout, the emphasis is on the economics governing the level and dynamics of asset prices.
faculty_bio: Jeffrey Rosenbluth is a Lecturer in the Practice of Management at Yale School of Management and a private investor. Yale’s official bio does not specify a particular research agenda or teaching focus, but highlights his experience as former Managing Director and head of Fixed Income Arbitrage at Salomon Brothers. He holds a BSE in computer science from the University of Pennsylvania, a PhD in mathematics from NYU’s Courant Institute, and an MBA from the University of Chicago; he is also a founding board member of Math for America and serves as a trustee or overseer at several institutions. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/jeffrey-rosenbluth))

Course Description: AM required.  AM student preregisted.  Open to other programs if space remains. Statistical Foundations is a practical, interactive course designed to equip students with the statistical tools necessary for modern financial data analysis. It provides a rigorous, hands-on exploration of advanced statistical methodologies, emphasizing regression techniques tailored for asset pricing research. Students will actively engage with complex financial phenomena throughout the course, using linear regression for prediction, inference, and other advanced topics. The course also introduces time series analysis and advanced estimation methods, such as Maximum Likelihood and Generalized Method of Moments, as crucial tools for aspiring financial analysts. Students are provided with ample opportunities to apply these tools to real-world financial data, using the statistical computing language R.
faculty_bio: Theis Ingerslev Jensen is an Assistant Professor of Finance at Yale School of Management, where he has been a faculty member since fall 2023. His research focuses on empirical asset pricing, particularly using new datasets related to subjective expectations, with data-intensive projects that apply advanced statistical methods such as machine learning. Jensen grew up in Denmark and earned a PhD in Financial Economics from Copenhagen Business School in 2023. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/theis-ingerslev-jensen))

Course Description: AM required.  AM student preregisted.  Open to other programs if space remains. This is a full 4 unit course that spans the fall-2 and spring-1 semesters. Empirical work is the foundation of great economics. Theory is also the foundation of great economics. Theorists work on closing the gap between theory and reality. Empiricists are explorers that map the unchartered territory between theory and reality. This is a division of labor view of Popper's philosophy of science. This course is designed to help build a skill set for pushing the empirical side of this proposition, particularly tailored to asset pricing research. AM required course (AM students preregistered).
faculty_bio: Bryan T. Kelly is the Frederick Frank ’54 and Mary C. Tanner Professor of Finance at Yale School of Management, Associate Director of its International Center for Finance, a Research Fellow at the National Bureau of Economic Research, and head of machine learning at AQR Capital Management. His research focuses on asset pricing and financial econometrics, including financial machine learning, volatility and tail risk, systemic banking risk, financial intermediation, and financial networks. He previously taught as a tenured professor at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business and has published in leading economics and finance journals. Kelly earned degrees from the University of Chicago, UC San Diego, and NYU Stern, and worked in investment banking at Morgan Stanley before pursuing his PhD. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/bryan-t-kelly))

Course Description: Financial markets play an important role in driving macroeconomic outcomes. Conversely, macroeconomic stabilization policy has become increasingly central to understanding asset prices. This course explores the rich set of interactions between financial markets, business cycles, and macroeconomic policy. We develop a framework for how asset prices and other shocks drive business cycles, and how central banks influence interest rates and asset prices to stabilize output and inflation. We also touch on other stabilization policies, including quantitative easing and financial-crisis interventions. We apply the framework to recent events—the Great Recession, the Covid-19 recession and recovery, the resurgence of inflation, bank runs, and the effects of tariffs and energy shocks on markets and policy. The course suits anyone seeking a macroeconomic perspective on financial markets.
faculty_bio: Alp Simsek is a Professor of Finance at Yale School of Management, where he has served since 2022. His research focuses on the connections between financial markets and the macroeconomy, including international finance, behavioral finance, beliefs, speculation, asset prices, monetary policy, and business cycles. Before Yale, he taught economics at MIT and Harvard, and he is a research associate at the National Bureau of Economic Research and a research affiliate at the Centre for Economic Policy Research. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/alp-simsek))

Course Description: This course taught by Jim Millar (formerly Princeton endowment) and Dean Takahashi (former Yale endowment), provides direct access to accomplished investors. Through case studies and simulated investment committee meetings, students will evaluate investment process and manager selection. This course is limited in capacity and requires a short pre-assignment. For more information about the assignment, MMS asset management students may contact: assetmanagement@yale.edu. The course is only open to SOM students in the Asset Management Master of Management Science program.
faculty_bio: Dean Takahashi is Professor Adjunct Emeritus of Management at Yale School of Management and Executive Director of the Carbon Containment Lab, which develops solutions for containing greenhouse gases. His teaching has focused on economics and endowment management, and he received Yale’s Merton J. Peck Prize for teaching excellence in 2018. Before turning to climate solutions, he spent more than three decades as a senior director in the Yale Investments Office, helping pioneer the influential “Yale Model” of institutional investing. He holds a B.A. in economics from Yale College and an MPPM from Yale SOM. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/dean-takahashi))

Course Description:
This course introduces a framework for investing based on fundamental analysis and evaluates investment opportunities through the lens of an equity investor. Although much of the material in this course has a strong academic foundation, the goal is to develop practical tools that the student can use immediately to improve their investment process and decision making in the real world.

The course will demonstrate how to determine a company’s fundamental value. Key inputs in the analysis will be the company’s level of profitability and financial returns, the duration of its competitive advantage, the value of its growth opportunity, the strength of its management team, and the risks inherent in the investment. These tools apply to public and private markets, and the course will show how to use the tools in each opportunity.

The course material will be delivered through lectures, exercises, readings, in-class discussions, and homework assignments; the last day of the course will be devoted to student presentations of an investment recommendation using the tools from the course.

Course Title: Emerging Market Central Banking and Financial Stability
Course Description: Central banks which had historically operated in the background came to the forefront in the wake of the Global Financial Crisis of 2008/09, playing an increasingly critical, and increasingly visible, role in supporting growth and stability across countries, regions and the world. Although central banks around the world are broadly similar in terms of their mandates and policy instruments, emerging market central banks are different by way of the policy trade-offs they face, the degrees of freedom available to them and the environment in which they operate. As the global economic center of gravity shifts towards the emerging world, an intelligent appreciation of emerging economy perspectives is imperative for acquiring a broad-based worldview of the global economy. In that light, the course will focus on the challenges and dilemmas of central banking in emerging markets. Drawing from international, particularly emerging market experience of the last two decades, the course will prioritize practice over theory and breadth over depth. Although no quantitative models will be used, an understanding of the concepts of macroeconomics is a prerequisite.
faculty_bio: Sigríður “Sigga” Benediktsdóttir is a Lecturer in Management at Yale School of Management and teaches part-time in its Master’s in Systemic Risk program. Her research focuses on international finance, particularly central banks and financial stability. She earned a PhD in economics from Yale in 2005 and has served as Director of the Financial Stability Department at the Central Bank of Iceland, an economist at the U.S. Federal Reserve Board, and an external expert for the IMF’s Financial Stability Assessment Program. She was also one of three members appointed to Iceland’s Parliamentary Special Investigation Commission on the causes of the 2008 banking collapse. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/sigridur-benediktsdottir))

Course Description:
This course is designed for students wishing to enter a field where fundamental firm valuation is a primary part of the job. For example, employment at a buy side firm such as a mutual fund, private equity, or employment in similar investment firm. If a career in investing is not what you are after, you may not want to take this class.

If you wish to take this class, you should be able to (1) calculate a company's beta, (2) calculate a company's discount rate, (3) conduct a discounted cash flow analysis, and (4) read a corporate 10-Q. If you cannot do any of these, then you should probably take the courses listed in the perquisites prior to taking Security Analysis.

During the semester students will learn to conduct in-depth financial analysis with the goal of valuing industries and their constituent firms. Over the semester you will be required to write and present four valuation reports: one industry report and three company reports. The students and faculty will discuss, comment on, and grade the written reports and class presentations. All members of the class are expected to actively participate in all sessions.

For this course you will be required to install an AI desktop app on your laptop.
faculty_bio: Matthew Spiegel is a Professor of Finance and Director of Graduate Studies at Yale School of Management. His research spans market microstructure, asset pricing, real estate, corporate finance, experimental economics, and dynamic models of competition and finance. He earned a Ph.D. in economics from Princeton University in 1987 and previously taught at Columbia University and the University of California, Berkeley. His work has received several best-paper awards, and he was named a Distinguished Scholar by the Eastern Finance Association in 2015. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/matthew-spiegel))

Course Description: Colloquium is a year-long course with 2 credits each semester (4 credits in total). Students will produce a thesis at the end of the colloquium. It will meet on Fridays.  Colloquium will consist of presentations by the students and outside speakers. On the weeks without any presentation, students will have individual meetings with his or her thesis advisor to discuss the thesis project. The colloquium is required for students in the MMS Systemic Risk program. It will be open to other Yale SOM students subject to permission from the instructor.
faculty_bio: Andrew Metrick is the Janet L. Yellen Professor of Finance and Management at Yale School of Management and serves as faculty director of the Yale Program on Financial Stability. His research and teaching focus on financial economics, including corporate finance, financial institutions, banking, and financial crises. Before joining Yale, he was a faculty member at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/andrew-metrick))

Course Description: The percentage of sales of successful business organizations tied to the successful introduction of new products and services is high. Given the fact that the failure rate of these introductions is also high, there is a need for tools and techniques to manage New Product Development (NPD) projects. This course will focus on the tools, techniques and best practices developed to support the initiation, planning, execution, monitoring and control of projects aimed at developing and marketing new products and services. Tuesdays, 16:00 - 18:00 (Israel time); Final class is 16:00 - 19:00 for presentations. Application link: https://event-reg.som.yale.edu/signup/NPD2024

Course Description: The premise of this class is simple: you never make a business decision in a vacuum. A wide range of political, geopolitical, social, environmental or technological forces influence your business environment. The better you understand your business environment, the better placed you are to formulate the business problem you're trying to solve. And the better positioned you are to identify the type of transformation you, your business or your activity, or even your industry (or the industry you are advising) needs to go through in order to meet its objectives. This class is designed to help you develop the appropriate toolbox and the appropriate change-making skills to rebuild and reinvent obsolete business models in a wide range of industries. Even in a world that is deeply changing, you can still have impact so long as you give yourself the means to harness and even influence global and business dynamics, as impressive as they might look on paper. Wednesdays at 8 am (EDT ) for 1.5 or three hours: No class on Nov 6 /1.5 h on Oct 9, on Oct 30, on Nov 13 and on Nov 20 /3h on Oct 16 and Oct 23/ 3h of asynchronous class between Oct 23 and Oct 30 /3h of asynchronous class between Oct 30 and Nov 13. Application link: https://event-reg.som.yale.edu/signup/ChangingBus
