Course Description: This course will discuss the economics of healthcare markets with a focus on understanding what is inefficient, what reforms and innovations might make things better and how strategic interactions among firms impact profits, health outcomes, and social welfare. Topics covered will include: measuring the value of health and medical care; the efficiency of US healthcare relative to other countries with different modes of delivery; the role of health insurance and competition among insurers; assessing healthcare delivery facilities such as hospitals and nursing homes; the healthcare workforce and physician behavior; pharmaceutical and medical device innovation; lessons from behavioral economics about the role of imperfectly informed consumers; the impact of the Affordable Care Act on health care in the US; and the role of AI in healthcare.

He is also a faculty research fellow at the National Bureau of Economic Research and received the 2024 John Bates Clark Medal for his contributions to economics. The goal is to introduce the types of questions asked in these areas, to think about how these questions may relate to each other and to questions in other disciplines, and to get you to think about issues you may want to research. The objective is to help you identify interesting, important, and researchable topics related to empirical financial accounting.

Course Description: This course is primarily designed for graduate students interested in econometric methods used in empirical research. The goal of this class is to provide an overview of different empirical methods, with an emphasis on practical implementation. I will provide a set of lecture slides and notes. There are additional background papers that are largely optional. More generally, this is a course where I focus on providing my understanding and intuition of empirical methods, as they are used by practicioners. This means that this is not a course where we will spend a lot of time on the formal details (beyond what is necessary), but instead focus on the intuitive framework that guides these papers. I'll also do my best to communciate how any of these topics fit together.

Course Title: Financial Econometrics and Machine Learning Part 2
Course Description:
Empirical work is the foundation of great economics. Theory is also the foundation of great
economics. Theorists work on closing the gap between theory and reality. Empiricists are
explorers that map the unchartered territory between theory and reality. This is a division
of labor view of Popper’s philosophy of science. This course is designed to help build a skill
set for pushing the empirical side of this proposition, particularly tailored to asset pricing
research. This is in large part a course in advanced statistical methods for finance. It is not a facts
course. I will bring in many empirical facts as we go. But the more important take-away for
you is a set of methods you can you to discover your own new facts.
faculty_bio: Bryan T. Kelly is the Frederick Frank ’54 and Mary C. Tanner Professor of Finance at Yale School of Management, Associate Director of its International Center for Finance, a Research Fellow at the National Bureau of Economic Research, and head of machine learning at AQR Capital Management. His research focuses on asset pricing and financial econometrics, including financial machine learning, volatility and tail risk, systemic banking risk, financial intermediation, and financial networks. He previously taught as a tenured professor at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business and has published in leading economics and finance journals. Kelly earned degrees from the University of Chicago, UC San Diego, and NYU Stern, and worked in investment banking at Morgan Stanley before pursuing his PhD. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/bryan-t-kelly))

Course Description:
The field of behavioral finance tries to make sense of investor behavior, financial markets, and corporate
finance using models that make psychologically realistic assumptions about the way people think, e.g., that
allow for less than fully rational thinking. In this course, we cover both the classic contributions to the field and
also the most recent research developments.

In this class, we explore foundational topics in behavioral economics, and discuss the dominant prescriptive models (which propose what decision makers should do) and descriptive models (which aim to describe what decision makers actually do). We incorporate perspectives from economics, psychology, philosophy, decision theory, and finance, and engage long-standing debates about rational choice.

The main objective of this 7-week course is to provide a deep, focused study on topics related to
morality in consumer decision making. The weekly readings are intended to provide PhD level coverage
of classic and current research on this topic.

This course covers analytical tools and topics that have not been discussed in previous
operations doctoral courses at Yale SOM. The emphasis is on approaches to modeling
and analyzing operational processes across various application areas, including supply
chains, service operations, retail operations, platform operations, and sustainable
operations. Students will explore key ideas and methodologies established in the
literature of Operations Research and Operations Management, understand the contexts
in which certain conventions have been developed, and learn how to build effective
mathematical models.  Part-1 and Part-2 can be taken independently. Students can enroll in both or only one.
faculty_bio: Uri Simonsohn is a Visiting Professor of Behavioral Science at Yale School of Management for the 2026–27 academic year and a Professor of Behavioral Science at ESADE Business School in Barcelona. His research focuses on judgment and decision-making, research methods, and the credibility and reproducibility of empirical findings. He teaches topics related to motivating behavioral change and improving people’s understanding of data through psychological research. Before joining ESADE, he was a professor at the Wharton School, where he served from 2003 to 2017. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/uri-simonsohn))

Course Description:
This course takes a mathematical look at how democratic institutions fairly allocate representation and aggregate preferences to make public decisions. We will begin with the foundational economics work in social choice theory on the design of voting systems. We will then progress through more modern developments from computer science on preference aggregation and fair allocation, including applications to AI and online platforms. The final part of the course will focus on institutions for distributing voting power. This includes traditional systems like apportionment and redistricting, as well as more radical proposals like liquid democracy and citizens assemblies. Throughout, particular focus will be given to designing efficient algorithms with theoretical guarantees.

This is a research-focused course geared toward PhD students in Operations, Computer Science, Economics, and related fields. Advanced undergraduates may enroll by instructor permission only, and will be held to the same standard as graduate students. The only firm prerequisite is that you must be very comfortable reading and writing mathematical proofs, specifically in areas of discrete mathematics. The course will also assume understanding of basic concepts in game theory (mixed strategies, Nash equilibria) and CS/OR (linear programming, NP-completeness).

Link to syllabus: https://jamie.tuckerfoltz.com/Teaching/AFDDM26_Syllabus.pdf

Course Title: Organizations and Management II: Macro and Meso
Course Description: This course provides an overview of the dominant perspectives within and current approaches to modern macro- and meso-organizational theory. We will also cover many of the current debates and developments in contemporary organizational research. The first section of the course will cover the major theoretical approaches that have been used to analyze organizations. In these sessions, we will read the classics as well as more recent papers that are largely in keeping with that week’s theoretical tradition. While legacies of each of these schools of thought can still be found, over time perspectives have combined and recombined and the boundaries between these traditions have become fluid. Accordingly, the latter section of the course is organized around active areas of macro and meso-organizational theory topics approached from a variety of theoretical and methodological traditions. For each area, we will read both foundational papers and more recent approaches with an eye towards understanding what makes for outstanding organizational research.
faculty_bio: Julia DiBenigno is a Professor of Organizational Behavior at Yale School of Management, with a courtesy appointment in Sociology. An organizational ethnographer and field researcher, she studies the sociology of work and occupations, collaboration across professional groups, upward influence and voice, and organizational change; she also teaches Managing Groups and Teams. Her background includes a PhD and MS from MIT Sloan, a summa cum laude psychology degree from Columbia, and prior consulting work in Deloitte’s Organization and Change practice. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/julia-dibenigno))

Course Description: The course objective is to learn a conceptual framework for analyzing and shaping negotiation processes and outcomes. Negotiation can be broken down into two basic activities: creating value and capturing value. Creating value is about making the pie bigger, while capturing value is about getting the largest possible slice for yourself. The course presents strategies for achieving both of these objectives at the same time. The course also helps students to develop a repertoire of negotiation strategies and skills. There are several opportunities to negotiate with classmates in a simulated environment.

Course Description: Costa Rica is a unique country in many respects. It is one of the few countries in the world without an army and is characterized by table political climate and high economic development. For instance, it has the highest public healthcare development in Latin America, with general insurance which covers 100% of the country and public universal education, which led to a life expectancy at birth of 80 years and a literacy rate of 96%. Further, for several years now, Costa Rica has run entirely on renewable energy and is the most diverse place in the world per square kilometer. This is also one of the few nations where 25% of the total territory is protected, and it hosts 5% of the world’s biodiversity. The course begins with three sessions of classroom study and culminates with a 10-day trip to Costa Rica. In Costa Rica, we will visit companies and meet business and political leaders, with an emphasis on the central role that foreign direct investment has had in the country’s growth. We will learn about coffee production and its central role in the country’s historical development. We will also visit natural reserves and animal sanctuaries in the country, which relies on tourism as its main source of hard currency and learn about their funding structure.
faculty_bio: Diana Van Patten is an Assistant Professor of Economics at Yale School of Management. Her research focuses on economic development, international trade, economic history, and the effects of foreign direct investment and trade in developing countries. She earned a PhD in Economics from UCLA in 2020 and previously was a postdoctoral associate at Princeton University’s International Economics Section. Originally from Costa Rica, she also holds a BSc from the Universidad de Costa Rica. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/diana-van-patten))

Course Description:
India’s economy has been growing and changing at an incredible pace in recent years. The goal of the India IE is to provide a broad introduction to some of the key driving forces behind this growth, as well as the associated complexities and challenges. 

We’ll be visiting Mumbai and Bangalore. These cities represent India’s financial and tech hubs, respectively, and the site visits will have a theme that (roughly) matches. What are the factors that have led Bangalore to become one of the world’s most important cities for innovation, for example, and what are the impacts of this transformation – from “Garden City” to “Silicon Plateau” – on the city and the country more broadly? How has the development of India’s financial sector shaped access to capital for conglomerates, high-tech entrepreneurs, rural small businesses, and everything in between? How is India’s business environment shaped by its legal, political, and cultural environment, and what might not be immediately apparent from an outsider’s perspective?
faculty_bio: Aneesh Raghunandan is an Associate Professor of Accounting at Yale School of Management, having previously been an assistant professor of accounting at the London School of Economics. His research examines environmental, social, and governance issues, firms’ political and economic connections to governments, corporate irresponsibility, and the reporting and consequences of corporate subsidies. He holds a PhD from Stanford Graduate School of Business and undergraduate degrees from Yale University, and he worked at the Federal Reserve between his undergraduate and graduate studies. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/aneesh-raghunandan))

Course Description:
In this course, we will dive into México’s history and explore how it has influenced its modern-day politics, artistic traditions, and cuisine. México was the center of several advanced Mesoamerican civilizations, such as the Aztec and Maya, before becoming the most important Spanish colony in the Hemisphere. México’s distinct blend of Spanish and indigenous cultures is still evident in its culture and traditions.

We will also delve into México’s economy, one of the largest economies in the world and one of the most relevant for international trade, particularly in North America. We will cover the reasons why México has been increasingly recognized as a growing hub for entrepreneurs, from technology and e-commerce to healthcare and finance.

This immersive international experience takes MBA students to two of China’s most dynamic cities—Beijing and Shanghai—to explore the intersection of business, technology, and culture in the world’s largest digital economy. With a focus on the rapidly evolving landscape of e-commerce, fintech, and technological innovation, this trip offers students a rare opportunity to engage directly with industry leaders and gain insights into China’s unique role in shaping global business trends.

Through visits to top-tier e-commerce companies, venture capital investors, cutting-edge manufacturers, banks and fin-tech companies, and innovative startups, students will explore the mechanisms driving China’s digital economy and its impact on global trade and consumer behavior. Students will also have the opportunity to engage with professionals in these sectors to discuss topics such as:

• The role of artificial intelligence and big data in consumer markets

• Cross-border e-commerce and regulatory challenges

• China’s economic growth and its contribution to the world economy

Course Description:
The International Experience – Japan (IE Japan), subtitled “Japan as Stakeholder Capitalism – Then, Now, and Future,” will focus on the country's business environment, with an emphasis on its long-standing tradition of stakeholder-oriented capitalism. This model, which prioritizes long-term value creation for a broad range of stakeholders beyond shareholders, will be juxtaposed with Japan's recent shift toward a more shareholder-centric economy. The course will also explore key challenges facing the country, including addressing the super-aging society, advancing gender equality, promoting diversity and inclusion, and incorporating youth perspectives within the context of a silver democracy.

The course will be of particular benefit to students interested in the relationship between business practices and societal impact. Beyond exploring Japan's stakeholder-oriented capitalism and economic landscape, the trip will also encompass cultural activities and sightseeing, providing a comprehensive experience in one of the world's most dynamic economies.

Today, South Korea is recognized as one of the powerhouses of the global economy, known for its multinational firms like Samsung, LG, Hyundai as well as cultural exports like K-pop and K-dramas. At the same time, it is a country situated in the most heavily-armed region of the world where conflicting interests of China, Russia, Japan, and the US have collided and shaped its politics and economy. It is also a country that underwent extremely rapid ascent into the world’s top-tier economy which, while benefitting the population as a whole, created societal tensions and related challenges. Through business meetings and other activities, in this IE trip you will have a chance to learn about many different aspects of Korean economy and culture as well as current challenges in the business environment, and get a better understanding of Korea’s role in the fast-changing international dynamics marked by structural shifts and uncertainties.

Course Description:
This course will investigate the changes in Ireland’s tax and regulatory environment that led to its economic growth. Among the issues we will discuss are its tax laws, and why they have led companies to move substantial parts of their operations to Ireland.

Through lectures, including some from members of the faculty at the University College Dublin, we will explore some of the political changes that led to the tax and regulatory changes. We will also look into the types of companies that moved their operations to Ireland. Plus, we will look at why Irish firms dominate the airline leasing industry.

Once in Ireland we will visit some of the companies covered in the lectures. They will provide insights into what their Irish operations look like and how they interact with parts of the company located elsewhere around the globe. Since St. Patrick’s Day falls in the middle of the trip, we will of course visit any number of cultural sites and offer people the opportunity to partake in the celebrations.
faculty_bio: Matthew Spiegel is a Professor of Finance and Director of Graduate Studies at Yale School of Management. His research spans market microstructure, asset pricing, real estate, corporate finance, experimental economics, and dynamic models of competition and finance. He earned a Ph.D. in economics from Princeton University in 1987 and previously taught at Columbia University and the University of California, Berkeley. His work has received several best-paper awards, and he was named a Distinguished Scholar by the Eastern Finance Association in 2015. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/matthew-spiegel))

Course Description: The purpose of this experiential course is to introduce participants to Bhutan through the conceptual framework of Gross National Happiness and the cultural context for business. In this small, unique and culturally rich country, students will have opportunities to learn about how modern governance is grounded in historical and Buddhist traditions; how culture and tradition are honored in practice and interwoven throughout all aspects of society; how protection of the natural environment is balanced with priorities for improving living conditions in rural and urban areas; and how economic growth opportunities are developed and sustained in the context of these other priorities for Bhutan’s wellbeing. Prior to travel, participants will study Bhutan in the context of the four pillars of Gross National Happiness and its nine domains (living standards, education, health, environment, community vitality, time use, psychological well-being, good governance, and cultural resilience and promotion). While on campus, course participants will have the opportunity to meet with experts to learn more about Bhutan’s society, culture, forestry and environment, religion and health care system.

Few economies on earth are undergoing a growth process as dynamic as those seen right now in many SubSaharan African countries. Many countries on the continent are characterized by expanding access technology, increasing educational attainment, urbanization, and a young population ready to take advantage of these changes. Yet at the same time, economic growth is uneven. Pockets of poverty exist next to expansive wealth, and youth unemployment reminds a persistently difficult issue to solve. This IE will delve into these issues in Nairobi, Kenya, our main location for the trip. Nairobi has developed as an important economic hub in East Africa.

The purpose of this course is to enhance the student’s capability as a manager and leader to take actions that align workers’ actions with organizational goals and objectives. The course begins by examining ways in which work and workforces are being transformed.  We next situate the manager’s relationship with the workforce in the broader context of the organization’s human resource strategy, emphasizing the importance of having a human resource strategy that is: aligned with the business strategy; internally consistent; and credible to the workforce. The course then examines in closer detail some of the main levers that managers and organizations can use to align workers’ objectives with those of the larger enterprise, including: job design; recruitment and selection; employee development and evaluation; extrinsic and intrinsic rewards; and organizational design. Throughout the course, we focus on how the management of employment relationships is influenced by diversity, the cultural context, and by values and ethics—those of the manager, as well as those of the larger organization.

Throughout the course, we focus on how the management of employment relationships is influenced by diversity, the cultural context, and by values and ethics—those of the manager, as well as those of the larger organization.

This class studies issues of idea generation, idea evaluation and development, creative projects, and fostering and sustaining innovation in organizations. Students are exposed both to the ways of thinking of innovators and to the promises and perils of interacting with and managing innovators. Students generate ideas in a number of contexts, and evaluate ideas that they and others have generated in terms of customer adoption (the market) and feasibility. They analyze innovation in a set of companies across sectors. Students also engage in a role-playing exercise to get a sense for how the innovator’s perspective interacts with a managerial perspective rooted in the other Organizational Perspectives courses.

The course broadens the traditional operations management course by including and emphasizing linkages to organizational behavior and workforce management, strategy, accounting, finance, and marketing. At its heart, this course is about using quantitative models to provide managerial insights. The framework for this course is simple: First, we focus on how work is organized and how processes are improved. At the next higher level, we consider the relationship among work centers, suppliers, and customers: the design and improvement of the supply chain. Finally, operations analysis influences and is influenced by the organization’s competitive strategy. While carrying out these activities, organizations need to continually improve manufacturing and service quality. These activities of process improvement, supply chain management, and quality management fundamentally involve issues of workforce management and organizational behavior and require understanding and applying capital budgeting and other accounting/finance tools, and coordination with the marketing function.
faculty_bio: Zhen Lian is an Assistant Professor of Operations Management at Yale School of Management and a faculty fellow at Yale’s Center for Algorithms, Data, and Market Design. Her research focuses on optimization, transportation, public policy, and online marketplaces, particularly ridesharing and the gig economy. She teaches Operations Engine and Advanced Business Analytics, and previously worked as a postdoctoral fellow at Lyft on driver pay and incentive design. Lian holds a PhD from Cornell University and bachelor’s degrees from Peking University; she also helped redesign San Francisco school schedules, generating substantial transportation-cost savings. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/zhen-lian))

This course considers groups within the firm tasked to raise money from different sources as well as manage different aspects of those funds within the organization. Many of these functions are concentrated within the office of the Chief Financial Officer (CFO), split between the Treasurer and the Controller. But many other functions are spread across the organization, principally in the hands of strategy groups and product managers. Topics include measuring corporate value creation; company valuation (discounted free cash flow, multiples); capital structure decisions (e.g., equity funding versus debt funding); capital budgeting (e.g., cash flow analysis, incorporating risk and taxes); the planning process; inputs for decision making; and performance evaluation.
faculty_bio: Menaka V. Hampole is an Assistant Professor of Finance at Yale School of Management, where she has served since fall 2023. Her research focuses on household finance and labor economics, particularly education financing and gender gaps in education and corporate leadership. She earned a PhD in finance from Northwestern University’s Kellogg School of Management, a master’s degree in economics from University College London, and a bachelor’s degree in economics from the University of Chicago. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/menaka-v-hampole))

This course develops a framework for understanding the causes and consequences of macroeconomic events in real time, a useful input to the management of any enterprise, local or global, profit or non-profit. We begin by defining basic national accounting identities and using these identities to compare countries’ economic structure and performance over time. We then consider models in which the choices of private and public agents interact to produce aggregate outcomes in response to policy or economic shocks. In developing and using these models, we will rely on numerous historical and contemporary examples, paying particular attention to current events.

Course Description: This course uses economic concepts to analyze strategic decisions facing an organization. Although the primary emphasis is on strategy at the individual business level, and the primary source of analytical methods is economics, other application areas (including finance, marketing, and organizational behavior) and other analytical perspectives are considered. The course provides the analytical and data analysis tools to balance the objectives, characteristics, and resources of the organization on the one hand, and the opportunities presented by the environment on the other. We will also focus understanding competitive interaction between firms, both in theory and in a variety of industry settings. The range of organizations studied includes nonprofits as well as for-profits. Class sessions are a mixture of case discussions and lectures. Written presentations of cases and participation are the classroom responsibilities of those taking the course.

Course Title: Market Failures and Economic Policy in Developing Countries
Course Description: This course provides a framework for understanding economic growth in developing countries. We start by building the workhorse model of economic growth used by international organizations like the World Bank, governments, and private firms to identify key drivers of long-term growth. Building on this foundation, we then explore how microeconomic market structures sometimes fail to deliver efficient outcomes, and how these "market failures" slow economic development. The class is designed to make students proficient in the quantitative tools used to analyze these issues and better understand challenges facing developing economies.

Launched in 2008 at the Yale School of Management, the Global Social Entrepreneurship (GSE) India course links teams of Yale students with social enterprises based in India. GSE is committed to channeling the skills of Yale students to assist Indian organizations to expand their reach and impact on “base of the pyramid” communities. Yale students partner with mission-driven social entrepreneurs (SEs) to focus on a specific management challenge that the student/SE teams work together to address during the semester.  GSE has worked with more than 50 leading and emerging Indian social enterprises engaged in economic development, sustainable energy, women’s empowerment, education, environmental conservation, and affordable housing. The course covers both theoretical and practical issues, including case studies and discussions on social enterprise, developing a theory of change and related social metrics, financing social businesses, the role of civil society in India, framing a consulting engagement, managing team dynamics, etc. The course will be taught by Asha Ghosh, Lecturer at SOM. The course meets on Wednesday afternoons 2:40 – 5:40 during Fall-2 and Spring-1. Students will travel to India to work on-site with their partner SEs, and for a convening of all the student/SE project teams, in mid- to late January 2026 for 10 days. As with the International Experience and the Global Network Immersion Week, students will be responsible for covering the costs of their round-trip airfare to India and related expenses (such as visa and immunizations). SOM students can draw on their available GSA days to offset in-country travel, hotel, and related costs. GSE has arrangements with Jackson and YSE to cover in-country costs for their students. Enrollment is by application only. Students accepted and enrolled in GSE will allocate 150 of their fall course bidding points towards the course. This is considered a 6 unit course that spans fall-2 and spring-1. It may not be taken as a half semester course. 2 units are applied in fall-2 and 4 units applied in spring-1.  If travel to India is cancelled the units will change from 4 to 2 in spring 2026.
faculty_bio: Asha Ghosh is a Lecturer in the Practice of Management at Yale School of Management, where she teaches Global Social Entrepreneurship in India. Her research interests include poverty alleviation, urban politics and policy, and community engagement in Asia. Before joining Yale, she worked in international development focused on decentralization and local governance in Asia and served as YSE’s Urban Program Manager from 2019 to 2024; she holds degrees from MIT and Tufts University. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/asha-ghosh))

Course Title: Applying a Social Innovation Lens to Social Movements
Course Description: This course applies social innovation tools and approaches to building strategies for social movements. We apply a combination of case-based and open discussion, utilizing tools such as stakeholder mapping, asset mapping, problem characterization, and theory of change. These tools are applied to a set of historical and current social movements to help understand institutional and non-institutional strategies for social change. Discussions blend policy, civic action, grassroots organizing, and innovation.
faculty_bio: Teresa Chahine is a Senior Lecturer in Social Entrepreneurship at Yale School of Management and Faculty Director of the Social Innovation Initiative at Yale Jackson School of Global Affairs. She teaches social entrepreneurship and researches tools for advancing social and environmental determinants of health, including how to finance, measure, and scale social impact. Chahine previously launched a public-health entrepreneurship program at Harvard and founded Lebanon’s first venture-philanthropy organization. She is also the author of *Social Entrepreneurship: Building Impact Step by Step*. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/teresa-chahine))

Course Description: Studies have shown that the average manager spends about two-thirds of his or her time interacting with others. It should be no surprise that skill in interpersonal relationships is one of the most frequent determinants of managerial success or failure. This course is designed to help students learn some of the skills necessary to build more open and effective working relationships. This course aims to increase student understanding of interpersonal and small group behavior. The central focus is to increase student ability to understand and diagnose interpersonal dynamics as well as to increase personal understanding of how she or he impacts others. While readings and group exercises are used to begin discussion, the core learning material emerges in small group interaction. Students learn how they function in small groups and how they relate to others from feedback and reaction of other class members. Students should be aware of the significant face to face time demands of this course. In addition to the standard class time, there will be a three hour weekly small group meeting immediately following the class meeting. Students are required to be present for both class times and the small group meeting each week during the course. Students enrolled in this section are required to attend a retreat. Students are required to attend the first two sessions to remain enrolled in the course.

Course Description: AM Required course. AM students only. AM students preregistered. Business is ripe with ethical challenges. This course is designed to help prepare you for those challenges. Throughout the course, we will use case studies, class discussion, and personal reflection to consider three aspects of business ethics. First, we will learn tools for thinking clearly about what is ethical and unethical in business. Drawing on philosophical perspectives, we will engage with modern controversies around pricing, privacy, product safety, and more. Second, we will explore the psychological and organizational factors that lead good people make ethically dubious decisions. Finally, you will have the opportunity to reflect on our own moral values and consider how you will uphold those values through the hazards and opportunities you will face in your career.

This course develops the foundations of competitive strategy through a rigorous analytical lens, with a focus on technology-intensive markets. Using economic models, we examine how firms gain and sustain advantage in environments shaped by innovation, data, and network effects. Topics include pricing, product positioning, bundling, auctions, and entry strategies, with special attention to the strategic dynamics common in tech sectors. The course also explores the role of antitrust policy in shaping competitive behavior. While case studies provide applied context, emphasis is placed on frameworks and techniques that generalize across industries and guide strategic thinking in rapidly evolving markets.

How much should I be saving at age 30? Is renting an apartment throwing money away every month? Which mortgage should I choose, and when should I refinance it? How much of my portfolio should be invested in stocks at age 50? How much can I afford to spend per year in retirement? This heavily quantitative course covers prescriptive models of personal saving, asset allocation, borrowing, and spending. It is designed to answer questions facing anybody who manages their own money or is a manager in an organization that is trying to help others manage their money. Emphasis will be on the U.S. context. Students will need to be comfortable with mathematical and statistical reasoning and spreadsheet modeling.

This course covers financial management from the perspective inside the corporation or operating entity. It covers aspects of corporate finance including capital structure, capital budgeting, cost of capital, valuation, risk management, and M&A. It uses examples, cases, and a final project to concretely map the lessons from class into corporate decision making in practice.

This course examines how firms and other organizations make decisions regarding funding sources, capital structure, and investment decisions. It builds upon the concepts from the core finance courses, using lectures to develop the theory, and problem sets and a raw case to provide applications. Topics covered include cost of capital, capital structure and valuation, bankruptcy and restructuring, leverage management, mergers and acquisitions, dividend and share repurchase policy, working capital management, and cross-border valuation. We will cover both traditional corporate finance topics and how they intersect with modern societal issues such as stakeholder interests, government bailouts, ESG, behavioral finance, tax evasion, cross-border operations, and financial innovation. The course will emphasize practical applications to current events.

This course provides a broad overview of investment management, focusing on the application of finance theory to the issues faced by portfolio managers and investors in general. Topics include the general tools of portfolio optimization and performance evaluation as well as the subject areas of asset allocation, equity investing in both efficient and inefficient markets, fixed income, alternative investments, international markets, and derivatives. The course includes lectures, guest speakers, cases, problem sets, and a final exam.

This course explores how organizations use predictive AI to make repeatable, data-informed decisions at scale and extract value from generative AI. Students learn to build and evaluate models using historical business data and translate predictions into actions, personalized experiences, and resource allocation. The course examines how predictive and generative AI complement one another: generative AI extracts information and creates new content and alternatives, while predictive AI estimates outcomes and guides which options to use, for whom, and under what conditions. Applications span customer management, marketing, pricing, forecasting, and operational planning, with examples including personalized targeting, content selection, and adaptive experimentation. Through lectures, business cases, vibe coding, and a team project, students develop practical skills in building AI solutions that connect data and models to measurable business outcomes.
faculty_bio: Tong Wang is an Assistant Professor of Marketing at Yale School of Management. Her research develops interpretable machine-learning models for business applications involving structured and unstructured data, including text and images. She teaches AI for Business Decisions and holds a Ph.D. in Computer Science from MIT. Her notable prior work includes crime-pattern detection adopted by the New York Police Department and an award-winning interpretable model for the 2018 FICO challenge. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/tong-wang))

Course Description: In today’s information economy companies have access to data about markets, products, customers, and much more. When deciding on strategic issues such as pricing, advertising or targeting these data can be very valuable to companies if used correctly. This course will provide you with the tools and methods that will allow you to leverage data to help shape a marketing strategy from a quantitative perspective. This course was previously titled Data-Driven Marketing.

Product management addresses the design and marketing of new products that solve problems consumers are willing to pay for. This course focuses on technology-driven products in B2C settings. Traditionally this referred to digital products (e.g., software apps), but increasingly includes physical products (e.g., electric vehicles). We will emphasize use of quantitative methods to analyze consumer feedback and product usage data to inform PM decisions.

We will cover specific PM issues across startup-stage, growth-stage, and enterprise-stage firms. Examples include how startups can achieve product-market fit, convert consumer needs to MVPs, and assess traction and when to pivot; how growth-stage firms can prioritize features, balance competing strategic objectives, and develop channels that scale to new markets; and how enterprise firms can conduct systematic product innovation and optimize products at scale.

The course will provide hands-on opportunities to apply course material on real PM problems from leading technology firms. We will accordingly cover technical skills required of PMs, including basics of technology-driven products (e.g., the software stack and modern cloud ecosystem); the interplay with design, UI/UX, and product marketing; and how to develop statistical hypotheses and conduct A/B tests.

Course Title: AI for Media, Entertainment, and Gaming
Course Description:
This course equips students with the tools and techniques of generative AI, focusing on its transformative applications for social media analysis and content creation. Emphasizing practical, hands-on learning, the curriculum trains students to leverage AI for analyzing, designing, and optimizing social media strategies. Key topics include:
1.	Building social media apps for sentiment analysis, influencer identification, and audience segmentation
2.	Harnessing generative AI to craft compelling text and visual content tailored to specific audiences
3.	Automating and optimizing social media campaigns to boost engagement and impact
Students will work extensively with advanced AI tools such as ChatGPT, gaining experience in analysis, content generation, and app development. Course assignments and projects are grounded in real-world social media datasets, culminating in a group project where students will create a social media application powered by generative AI.
As a fully project-based course, there are no exams. The assignments and projects are designed to be accessible to all students, regardless of prior coding experience, making it an ideal opportunity to develop expertise in applying generative AI to the dynamic field of social media.
faculty_bio: Tauhid Zaman is an Associate Professor of Operations Management at Yale School of Management, where he also serves as Lecturer in Management and Special Advisor for AI Initiatives. His research uses probabilistic models, network algorithms, and modern statistical methods to address operational problems involving social-network data, including content popularity, online extremism, and user geolocation. He also studies data-driven startup investing, choice modeling, algorithmic sports betting, and biometric data. Zaman earned his BS, MEng, and PhD in electrical engineering and computer science from MIT, completing his doctorate in 2011. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/tauhid-zaman))

Course Description: This course examines the U.S. education system through the dual lenses of policy research and real-world decision-making. Topics will include balancing local, state, and federal authority; teacher, school, and district accountability; school choice and school vouchers; early childhood education; higher education access; and higher education finance. For each topic, we will consider the available evidence base in the context of a specific policy case study, highlighting both the use of evidence in policy design and the practical challenges of leading organizations through policy implementation. Assessment will be based on class participation, written memos, and student presentations.
faculty_bio: Seth Zimmerman is the Eli and Edythe Broad Professor of Economics, Education, and Management at Yale School of Management and faculty research director of The Broad Center. His research focuses on labor economics, public finance, and the economics of education, including educational attainment, returns to education, upward mobility, inequality, and school-choice policy. He earned his PhD, MPhil, and MA from Yale University and his BA from Dartmouth College. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/seth-zimmerman))

Doug Kysar is the Joseph M. Field ’55 Professor of Law at Yale Law School. His research and teaching focus on torts, environmental law, climate change, and the regulation of risk. He holds degrees from Harvard University and Yale Law School and has served on the Yale faculty since 2000. ([law.yale.edu](https://law.yale.edu/doug-kysar))

Course Title: Economic Evolution of the Latin American and Caribbean Countries
Course Description:
Economic evolution and prospects of the Latin American and Caribbean (LAC) countries. Topics include the period from independence to the 1930s; import substitution and industrialization to the early 1980s; the debt crisis and the "lost decade"; reform and disappointment in the late 1980s and the 1990s; exploration of selected episodes in particular countries; and speculations about the future. 
Prerequisities: intermediate microeconomics and macroeconomics.
This course is cross-listed from the Jackson Institute and will follow their academic calendar.
faculty_bio: Ernesto Zedillo is the Frederick W. Beinecke Professor in the Field of International Studies at Yale, with appointments at the Yale School of Management and Jackson Institute for Global Affairs, and he directs the Yale Center for the Study of Globalization. His research and teaching focus on globalization, international economics, and public policy. A Mexican economist and statesman, he served as Mexico’s president from 1994 to 2000 after holding senior government positions, including secretary of education and secretary of programming and budget. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory))

Course Description: Data alone is not always enough to drive insight or impact. Data surrounds us, and while transforming raw data through analytics can yield discovery, increasing there is a need to not only process it but also present it in a meaningful way to maximize actionable insight. The course will revolve around teaching students how to represent information and data in a visual and impactful ways by translating the study of grammar of graphics into effective graphs, charts, graphics, images to transform data into impactful data stories. Students will primarily work in excel, R and adobe illustrator but will be exposed to other data visualization tools and examples of these tools in action from guest speakers and lectures. The structure of the course content will include specific information visualization practices alongside storytelling methods and design strategies for developing visual narratives to drive impact. The students will apply these techniques into specific tools (including RawGraphs, Datawrapper, Flourish, and Tableau) through assignments that culminate in a data visualization project of their choosing (either from course options, a Board Fellows engagement, Social Impact client data, or data from another source).
faculty_bio: Kate Cooney is a Senior Lecturer in Social Enterprise and Management at Yale School of Management and the founding director of its Inclusive Economic Development Lab. Her research examines the intersection of business and social sectors, with current interests including social finance, inclusive economic development in American cities, and social-sector data visualization and storytelling. She teaches community economic development and urban poverty, previously served on the Boston University faculty, and holds a PhD and MSW from UCLA’s Luskin School of Public Affairs. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/kate-cooney))

Course Description: This is designed to be a "second" game theory course. We build on the learnings from introductory game theory courses like ECON 159/GLBL 159, and MGT 822. The course aims to introduce important ideas and tools from game theory, and use them to answer questions in social sciences, law, and business. For instance, how does information get sold and used to persuade? How do we think about the efficiency and equity of allocations? How do sellers decide the best format for an auction to sell a good? Does requiring unanimous verdicts guarantee that the innocent will not be convicted? What causes bank runs? When do we see price wars? The underlying ideas will include games of incomplete information, mechanism design, common knowledge and high-order reasoning, and repeated games.
Final Exam: YC will schedule if there is one
faculty_bio: Benjamin Polak is the William C. Brainard Professor of Economics and Management at Yale School of Management and a professor of economics at Yale. His research and teaching focus on microeconomic theory, particularly game theory, decision theory, and strategic decision-making. He earned his Ph.D. in economics from Harvard University and has held major academic leadership roles at Yale, including serving as Dean of Yale College. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/benjamin-polak))

Course Description:
Class attendance is mandatory, including the first day.  Those who miss the first day of class will be dropped from enrollment. This course takes a comprehensive view of the value-adding impact of top corporate leaders and how they revolutionize their enterprises, their industries, and the world economy. The subject matter will embrace and integrate such broad key dimensions of strategic change as economic context, shifting markets, emerging technologies, corporate life stage, company culture, and corporate governance together with the character, skill-set, and life stages of individual leaders.   
 The course mission involves three equally important goals. The first is to help students anticipate the multi-dimensional cross-disciplinary aspects of successful planned change from strategic systems to group dynamics and individual psychology. A second is to appreciate the consequences of the unintended effects of strategic change initiatives on work communities and societies at-large. The last is to provide students with an overview of the contemporary industry-specific challenges in an effort to highlight the varied leadership values and skills that are not always apparent as corporations make acquisitions or managers select careers. The course materials used to fulfill this mission require students to be comfortable with a wide variety of learning tools including: research articles; case studies; current industry periodicals; spirited class discussion; role playing; video; and frequent prominent industry leaders as class visitors. 
 Following an overview that builds an analytic framework for the course, the key dimensions of strategic change will be examined through a sequence of industry-by-industry settings including: professional services; financial services; retail; e-commerce; communications and media; recreation and travel; government and nonprofit; industrial and consumer products. Toward the close, the course will return to cross-industry change leadership and challenges such as executive succession, life stage imperatives, and ethical dilemmas. There are 5 seats reserved for MBA first years.  You will need to bid to enroll.

We build on the learnings from introductory game theory courses like ECON 159/GLBL 159, MGT 620 and MGT 822. The course aims to introduce important ideas and tools from game theory, and use them to answer questions in social sciences, law, and business. The underlying ideas will include games of incomplete information, mechanism design, common knowledge and high-order reasoning, and repeated games.

His research and teaching focus on microeconomic theory, particularly game theory, decision theory, and strategic decision-making. He earned his Ph.D. in economics from Harvard University and has held major academic leadership roles at Yale, including serving as Dean of Yale College. Course Description: This course provides a transactional and numerical understanding of M&A to a level of knowledge that is expected within leading Wall Street investment banks and private equity firms, using a combination of conceptual learning, real case studies and simple modelling in Excel. It also covers the strategic and executional aspects of M&A as they relate to the identification and implementation of transactions, so as to optimise the results from a corporate finance and top management perspective. M&A represents one of the largest areas of corporate finance activity, with as much as $74.9 trillion value of transactions completed between 2000 and 2023. This course is therefore of high relevance to anyone interested in pursuing a career in Finance, Management Consulting or Corporate Management.

Like an epic quest, the rite of passage through Yale's School of Management to a professional career often follows a pattern of initiation -- separation, transformation through ordeal, and embarkation into a new stage of life. We will examine ideas about the quest for a fulfilled life as expressed by respected religious and philosophical figures such as Confucius and Jesus as well as diverse modern thinkers. To provide a framework for finding and articulating an authentic leadership vision, we will also consider excerpts from initiation stories, including Homer's The Odyssey, Shakespeare's King Lear, Willa Cather's My Antonia, and Hemingway's The Nick Adams Stories. We will look beyond simply defining what we want in order to discover what is worth wanting. Through a series of small writing assignments, students will map out a vision for a life worth living by reflecting upon how we as leaders can authentically navigate a professional career in business while grappling with the inevitable realities of vulnerability, loss, and suffering encountered along the way. Compass in hand, we step forward with confidence.

John H. Augustine is an accomplished investment banker and scholar with nearly four decades of experience advising colleges, research universities, academic medical centers and significant foundations and nonprofits on their most complex financial challenges. As Managing Director and head of Barclays’ Higher Education and Academic Medical Center Finance Group, John builds strong client relationships and enduring trust with senior leaders and their teams, guiding client organizations through pioneering capital strategies that offer innovative solutions to business problems. A Fulbright Scholar at Merton College, Oxford with a PhD in English Literature alongside his MBA and MDiv from Yale, John brings a rare combination of financial rigor and deep commitment to the academic mission, reflected in his ongoing service as an Associate Fellow of Pierson College and Trustee of the California State University Foundation.

Course Title: Law, Risk, and the Corporate Manager
Course Description:
Virtually every organizational decision—whether in consulting, finance, private equity, tech, or startups—takes place within a legal framework. Yet many leaders encounter the law only when something goes wrong. This course introduces the core legal structures that shape American business while emphasizing how executives use legal reasoning as a strategic tool to allocate risk, structure transactions, protect innovation, and avoid catastrophic liability.

Through case discussions and applied exercises, students will examine contracts, corporate governance, intellectual property, regulatory oversight, and civil liability. The course emphasizes practical judgment: how leaders identify legal risk early, communicate effectively with counsel, and incorporate legal reasoning into strategic decision-making.

The traditional framework for thinking about financial markets assumes that all market participants are fully rational. The past two decades have seen the emergence of an important new paradigm, behavioral finance, which argues that many financial phenomena are the result of less than fully rational thinking and which draws on psychology to understand the ways in which people are not fully rational. This course provides an introduction to the field. We revisit basic topics in finance from a behavioral finance perspective: topics related to markets (stock market fluctuations, popular investment strategies, bubbles); topics related to investor behavior (poor investment decisions by households); and topics related to corporate finance (security issuance, mergers and acquisitions). A running theme in the course is that knowledge of behavioral finance is essential for anyone who seeks a full understanding of modern financial markets. There are no prerequisites – the course is self-contained – but some students like to take it in conjunction with the Spring-1 course MGT 854, Behavioral Economics."

Equity Capital Markets is an academic course built upon the same principles as the MGT 635 M&A taught by Simon Hirst in the Spring Semester-1 of 2024 and 2025, and again in 2026. As such, it teaches the complex conceptual and numerical transactional and structural aspects of Equity Capital Markets in a manner that builds upon students’ theoretical knowledge and stretches their learning curve. The teaching methodology includes (i) understanding the concepts of ECM; (ii) a discussion of these concepts in the context of numerous real-life cases studies; and (iii) interpreting the numerical paradigms of these different transaction structures using simple Excel Model templates designed and built by the professor. Simon Hirst has taught this subject extensively for 10 years in Europe, although he would be adjusting these materials and adding new case studies specifically for the sophisticated student audience at YSOM.

Founder’s Practicum provides active, real-world founders the opportunity to work on their start-up ventures while enrolled at SOM as students. Over the course of the semester, students develop and test hypotheses about their customers, products, and markets. Depending on the student, this can include building and distributing product; gathering feedback from key customers/stakeholders; researching the competition; developing pricing and sales strategies; and finding investors. Teams/students are not merely thinking about launching ventures; they are actively working on their ventures and receiving feedback from mentors, stakeholders and their classmates. It is an intense and transformational experience. Admission is by application.
Final Exam: yes for presentations both oct and dec

Course Description: This 6-credit, project-based course gives students exposure to some of the complex questions and challenges on the minds of top marketing executives today. In this experiential learning course, each small group of students will be paired with a leading corporation and will work alongside experienced faculty and advisors to tackle a current business challenge. This course applies theories in Behavioral Science to help uncover the drivers of consumers’ beliefs and motivations. These insights will then be used to meet the real-world marketing challenge and results will be presented to high-level managers within the participating firm. Students will learn how to go from problem to solution in real-world situations. Each five-member student team will meet at least once per week as a group, and will attend weekly faculty advising meetings. Approximately 10 mandatory lectures / course events will take place on Wednesdays from 5:45-7:15PM EST, dates TBC. This course is by application only; there are no bid points assigned. See YCCI site for more information: https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research-centers/centers-initiatives/center-for-customer-insights/discovery-projects

Course Description: If Amazon sent a warning to customers with the top-3% of product returns last quarter, what analysis would you request to learn whether the warning worked and should be repeated? How could the team running A/B tests misuse statistics, 'p-hack', to show something that's not true, and how could you detect and prevent it? This course arms you with the tools to answer questions like these. It focuses on intuition, on going from statistical results to critical thinking, rather than form data to statistical results. We will not write code, but will ask AI to do so on occasion.
faculty_bio: Uri Simonsohn is a Visiting Professor of Behavioral Science at Yale School of Management for the 2026–27 academic year and a Professor of Behavioral Science at ESADE Business School in Barcelona. His research focuses on judgment and decision-making, research methods, and the credibility and reproducibility of empirical findings. He teaches topics related to motivating behavioral change and improving people’s understanding of data through psychological research. Before joining ESADE, he was a professor at the Wharton School, where he served from 2003 to 2017. ([som.yale.edu](https://som.yale.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/uri-simonsohn))

Course Description: This course studies business model design as a strategic choice: how a firm decides what value to create, for whom, and how to capture a share of it. The course objective is to develop a framework for understanding why a company makes money the way it does, what the alternatives were, and what makes a model durable under competitive pressure. Each session examines one company in depth, from Costco's membership model and Visa's payment network to TSMC's pure-play manufacturing and Nvidia's repeated platform reinventions, using episodes of the Acquired podcast as the primary course material in place of traditional written cases. Recurring themes include value creation and value capture, pricing as a design instrument, vertical integration versus ecosystem strategies, network effects and switching costs, and business model evolution over time. Coursework consists of class participation and short analytical memos.

New Digital innovations (e.g., blockchain, Artificial Intelligence), legal changes (e.g., legalized gambling, autonomous vehicle regulation) and consumer interest (e.g., e-commerce, sports anywhere) together with immediate digital scale and computing improvements (e.g., quantum computing) have allowed significant digital disruptions across multiple industries.

The digital economy has grown rapidly since the first wave in the 1990s when the internet opened new opportunities to provide information, services, and to buy physical goods - many failed (e.g., eToys, B2B marketplaces) or faded over time (e.g., Excite), but they proved digital could work and several thrived (e.g., Amazon, Google, Expedia).  Post the early 2000s bubble, we saw a second wave of digital disruption where a few specific verticals (e.g., news, media, retail, travel) saw major transformations led by a second wave of “Born of the Web” companies (e.g., Facebook, Twitter, YouTube, Etsy, AirBnB, Uber).  The 2010s saw digital accelerate and expand beyond the first impacted industries into food (curbside pick up / delivery vs. eating out and/or going to grocery store), entertainment (streaming vs. TV/movies, highlights vs. watching live sports), auto (online purchase vs. dealers), and branded apparel (Direct to Consumer vs. physical retail).  The 2020s have accelerated these trends and added new B2C industries (e.g., electric and autonomous vehicles, cryptocurrency, online gambling) and the development of B2B2C industries (e.g., embedded insurance, marketplaces).

This class will focus (1) identifying technology changes that can create windows for disruption, (2) determining how to pick which opportunities to pursue and (3) how new entrants and incumbents drive to win in these new spaces.

The primary objective of this course is to enable students who have some facility with fundamental management principles and financial analysis, garnered through exposure in other relevant courses, to focus on specific demands of the entrepreneurial process. It is important to note that this course is not aimed as a practical guide to entrepreneurship – we will not write business plans, for example. Rather, its goal is to discuss current approaches to entrepreneurship in management, psychology, sociology, and economics. Having said this, if your goal is to start your own company, I am sure that the theoretical approaches that we will cover will help you make more informed decisions.

This course will use a mixture of case studies, simulation exercises, and academic articles to explore essential elements of the entrepreneurial process. During the course we will explore topics such as: i) the founding of a new venture, ii) deciding to be a solo-entrepreneur or part of a founding team, and iii) developing a prototype. We will also discuss the theory and practice of obtaining financial resources and growing the venture. Finally, we will discuss long-term plans and possible exit strategies.

The primary objective of this course is to enable students who have some facility with fundamental management principles and financial analysis, garnered through exposure in other relevant courses, to focus on specific demands of the entrepreneurial process. It is important to note that this course is not aimed as a practical guide to entrepreneurship – we will not write business plans, for example. Rather, its goal is to discuss current approaches to entrepreneurship in management, psychology, sociology, and economics. Having said this, if your goal is to start your own company, I am sure that the theoretical approaches that we will cover will help you make more informed decisions.

Trust in science among the public is at a recent-historic low, and there are powerful forces working to keep it that way. If experts do not actively engage in the information landscape, their work risks being undone or lost. If they interact in the wrong ways, they could end up only contributing more to the chaos and division that currently characterize the information landscape. Opting out is not an option; we all have public faces now, and the question is how best to develop and utilize them. Given the state of division and distrust that threaten science, it should likely be among the aspirations of every graduate with an interest in healthcare management, science, medicine, and/or public health to have some part in shaping narratives that promote health and fact-based discourse over angry, divisive stagnation. This course invites students to study ways in which it can be done, and to reflect on their own potential, and to try out different techniques and different platforms—to begin to find their public voice. To see what works for some messages and some communicators, and what fails, and why. 
 
 The course will introduce and study the increasingly broad array of tools to engage in public discourse, to reach people outside of their immediate circles of professional contacts, and to influence the lives of many. It is predicated on the idea that science cannot be conceived as a system by which knowledge emanates outward (much less downward) from academia, or it will cease to reach people and to affect the world, but only exacerbate distrust and claims of elitism. Rather science can only exist as an active process of communication between researchers and the public. This is how trust is built and the learning process is most effective, as a mutual, shared endeavor. This is a widely held conception of science, and yet the actual methods of such engagement are overlooked or ignored by many in the health sciences. 
 
 This course is not prescriptive, but is meant to engage critically with modes of communication and shaping discourse. The course will equip students to critically analyze emerging methods of health-oriented communication. It will offer a survey of many approaches wherein students will develop an understanding of the canonical paths to writing for large audiences (op-eds, long-form journalism)—as well as explore how narratives emerge over time in much smaller and more personal scales. We will study the role that experts play in creating media on their own platforms and by working with media outlets as either sources or contributors, consultants or editors or publishers.  It is critical that not all experts communicate in the same styles and on the same platforms. Writing an op-ed in The New York Times is valuable, for example, but the ability to do that is just one tool in what needs to be an arsenal of ways of reaching people across cultural, socioeconomic, ideological, intellectual, and educational backgrounds."

This course will provide students with an opportunity to explore being a CEO, owner, entrepreneur of an emerging small or medium enterprise. The course will examine operational, organizational and financial issues that are prevalent in developing small and medium businesses. Cases will examine startups, acquired companies, family businesses and sponsored businesses (private equity owned). Not for profits will also be considered. The course will focus on the developing and adolescent stages of the business – beyond start up and prior to maturity or exit. The size of the businesses will roughly be $2m to $100m in annual revenue. Students will discover that organizations of this size can be resource constrained, lack infrastructure and will require innovative and creative solutions and strategies to grow and create value.
The general nature of the course will give students a complete view of the enterprise and an understanding of what choices can be made to grow the enterprise, improve the enterprise, finance the businesses and create value. Students will be required to assess the current situation of the enterprise and its leader, diagnose the challenges and opportunities and make specific recommendations and action plans with quantitative and qualitative support. Students will learn new skills and concepts while analyzing the cases and will also draw upon the Core foundation. The course will provide students with an opportunity to understand what it is like to lead, run, grow and manage a smaller organization and how this might fit as a career choice. This course will require active participation in class. Please be prepared and committed to participate in class. If you do not enjoy participating in class, this might not be the right course for you. Official and unofficial auditing is not permitted. Please see the Registrar’s Office (not the instructor) for all enrollment, registration, and auditing questions.
faculty_bio: A. J. Wasserstein is the Eugene F. Williams, Jr., Senior Lecturer in the Practice of Management at the Yale School of Management.
